name: Backbone Ridge
approach: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Colchuck Lake Trail (~4 mi, 2,280 ft gain) → around the lake and up the moraine to the route base (roughly 200 ft left of Serpentine Arête); initial bushwhacking on brushy ledges until the party cliffs out and traverses up/right toward the ridge crest.
descent: Most parties descend the east ledges and sandy summit gully toward Aasgard Pass and down to Colchuck Lake. When the upper descent gully is icy (common late season), rappel instead — two rappels on a 70m rope (60m works) using rock anchors to avoid the ice slope, with a documented rappel station near 47.479°N, 120.832°W. Watch for loose rock and verify anchor integrity on any rappel here — parties have found the anchors below the first station poor enough to turn round and downclimb instead, and the second rappel runs directly over a loose flake big enough to kill, with the standard walking descent passing below it.
hazards: Rockfall
loose rock on the descent, including at rappel anchors — verify integrity
the Fin's traverse pitch is highly exposed with minimal protection

waysIn.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; light crampons and an axe are worth carrying earlier for the snow patch below the base and for the descent gully
waysIn.notes:
Identical to the Serpentine approach as far as the moraine: Stuart Lake Trailhead, left at the junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, about four miles and 2,280 ft to Colchuck Lake — roughly an hour and a half of uphill from the trail junction. Fill water and use the toilet near the lake's south end; there is nothing above.

Past the campsites you drop out of the forest into large talus blocks and follow cairns, then pick up the climbers' path along the moraine, passing a small creek on your left, until the face opens up in front of you.

A perennial snow patch sits below the start; its size varies year to year and it is usually short enough that crampons and axe are a convenience rather than a necessity by midsummer. Above it, a loose gully and gravel ledges lead to the scrambling.

Parties report roughly four and a half to five and a half hours from car to the first roped pitch.
hazards: Perennial snow patch below the base, size varies year to year
Loose gully and gravel ledges on the approach scramble
Serious rockfall exposure on the lower face; a rockfall accident has occurred here
Cliffing-out on the bushy ramps is normal but disorienting for a party expecting a clean line
The standard descent gully ices up late season, which changes it from a walk-off into a rappel

name: Pandora's Box (W Couloir)
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly 4.3-4.4 miles and about 2,200 ft of gain (2-2.5 hours). Unlike the Aasgard Pass routes, continue around the lake's west/south side toward the Colchuck Glacier below the Colchuck-Dragontail col. Ascend talus and then the glacier itself - early season mostly snow, becoming firmer neve/ice with exposed talus by mid-to-late season; the glacier's east lobe is generally reported free of significant crevasses but can be hard enough to want crampons and an axe. Climb the glacier to Colchuck Col; the couloir entrance for Pandora's Box (the W Couloir) is a couple hundred feet left (east) of the col itself and climbs to a notch in the ridge. Total approach 3-4 hours. Hazards: firm morning snow/ice on the glacier approach, and the couloir is a fall-line funnel for rockfall/icefall from the terrain above, so an early start to beat sun-loosened debris and softening snow matters.
descent: From the top of the couloir/Pandora's Box, descend left and traverse northeast to the true summit (some parties rope up for this exposed traverse), or alternatively exit about 30 ft below the notch, scramble Class 4 rock roughly 20 ft, and follow the ridge left to the top. From the summit, the standard descent is southeast to a saddle, then east across a long snow slope to Aasgard Pass, then down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) to Colchuck Lake - stay climbers' left near the granite walls and beware drifting climbers' right into cliffs. Crampons/axe are recommended into mid-summer; early season the descent can largely be glissaded. No rappels are needed on this standard summit-and-Aasgard-Pass finish. If a party instead retreats directly back down the couloir rather than topping out, downclimbing steep snow/ice or building an improvised rappel off natural gear (slung chockstones or horns) in the couloir could become necessary - this specific scenario is not recorded anywhere but is a reasonable contingency to plan for in a steep snow couloir.
hazards: rockfall in the couloir, especially with parties above
avalanche terrain early season after storm loading
steep, sometimes icy snow requiring solid self-arrest technique

waysIn.name: Colchuck Glacier to Colchuck Col
waysIn.season: May-Jul, best on a firm consolidated snowpack
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — roughly 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft.

This one does not use Aasgard Pass. Continue around the lake's west and south side toward the Colchuck Glacier under the Colchuck-Dragontail col. Ascend talus and then the glacier: mostly snow early in the season, turning to firmer neve and ice with talus showing through by late season. The east lobe is generally reported free of significant crevassing but gets hard enough to want crampons and an axe. Late in the season a band of blue ice can span most of the snowfield, and parties have found a continuous snow finger on the right to get past it.

Allow three to four hours from the lake.
hazards: Firm morning snow and ice on the glacier — crampons and axe
A blue-ice band across the snowfield late in the season
The couloir is a fall-line funnel for rockfall and icefall from above — start early, before sun-loosened debris and softening snow

name: West Route / Standard Scramble
approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft, at the end of Phelps Creek Road/FR-6211), follow the Phelps Creek Trail (FST 1511) north up the east side of Phelps Creek through old-growth and second-growth forest. The trail crosses several small side streams (reliable water the whole way) and, in years with heavy winter avalanche activity, threads through 'graveyards' of downed timber deposited across the tread by slide paths off the Ten Peak/Chipmunk Creek slopes to the west — expect some minor scrambling over debris and a couple of ankle-to-shin stream fords early season. The trail climbs gently, gaining roughly 1,900 ft over about 6-7 miles to reach Spider Meadow (~5,400 ft), a broad subalpine meadow with good campsites and the last easy, reliable water before the basin. At the head of the meadow the trail forks: the left branch continues toward Spider Gap/Larch Knob, while climbers bound for Dumbell should watch for the unsigned climbers' path (old FST 1511A) that splits right (east) about 0.3 mile into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in upper Phelps Basin (~6,000 ft), 8-9 miles and roughly 2,500 ft above the trailhead. From camp, leave the last of the boot path and head east/northeast up along a tumbling side creek that cuts through an otherwise cliffy face, following a broad talus-and-scree gully on the south side of Dumbell. Grass and heather give way to talus and (through roughly mid-August) moderate snow as you climb into the basin directly south of the summit. Gain the southeast ridge/shoulder at a distinct notch, then work up steep snow or a loose scree-and-talus gully 100-200 yards left (west) of the notch to reach a system of ledges; these ledges zig-zag up onto the west ridge, which is then followed a few hundred feet of easy but moderately exposed Class 3 scrambling to the 8,421-ft summit. Route-finding is the main crux — several parallel gullies and ledge systems exist and it's easy to get cliffed out on the wrong one — and loose rock, lingering steep snow (an ice axe and sometimes crampons are worth carrying into July), and a reported unstable, truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully are all real hazards on this line. A longer alternate approach reaches the same basin from the east via Railroad Creek/Lyman Lake and Spider Gap out of Holden Village on Lake Chelan — considerably longer, typically used by parties already doing the Lyman Lake/Spider Gap loop.
descent: Descent is a reversal of the ascent line, down the west ridge and the ledge/gully system back into the south-facing basin above Phelps Basin — there is no fixed rappel gear anywhere on the route and no rappelling is required in normal (mid-to-late-summer) conditions. From the summit, downclimb the Class 3 west ridge scrambling back to the ledges; parties note it's easy to end up above short cliff bands here, so look for the same 'hidden' ledge/gully used on the way up rather than improvising a new line — a party that took a slightly different slanting ledge below the summit found it went, but cleaner options may exist. Downclimb the loose scree/talus gully back to the notch on the southeast shoulder, cross any remaining snow patch (crampons/axe useful into mid-summer), then descend the broad talus-and-scree gully into upper Phelps Basin, glissading or plunge-stepping any snow that remains for quick progress. From Phelps Basin, pick up the climbers' path back to the main Phelps Creek Trail (FST 1511) at Spider Meadow and hike out the way you came. The main descent hazards are loose rock and rockfall onto parties below in the gully, exposure on the ledge traverses, and — for parties who linger — losing daylight on a long, mostly off-trail descent; this is set up as a car-to-car or one-camp objective, not a route with roped rappels.
hazards: loose rock and rubble on the south-face gully and summit ledges
exposed Class 3-4 steps near the notch and west ridge
sun-softened afternoon snow with wet-slide/rockfall risk on the approach gully (in 2016 a truck-sized snow block released off a rock slab)
route-finding confusion — similar-looking notches/false summits near the top have led parties astray
long committing approach with no reliable cell coverage
early-season snow requiring axe/crampons through June/early July
Phelps Creek fords can be difficult at high flow or early in the season

waysIn.name: Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to Spider Meadow and upper Phelps Basin
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep. Before that the approach gully and the upper basin are full snow, wanting an axe and often crampons; snow returns to the upper mountain by late September
waysIn.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft at the end of FR-6211, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the east side of the creek. It climbs gently — roughly 1,900 ft over five or six miles — through old and second growth, with several small side streams giving reliable water the whole way. After a heavy avalanche winter the tread threads graveyards of downed timber pushed across it from the slopes to the west.

Spider Meadow near 5,150-5,400 ft is the last easy, reliable water. Walk the length of the meadow to its head, where the trail forks. The fork is unsigned: the left branch carries on toward Spider Gap and Larch Knob, and the Dumbell path is the right-hand one, an old climbers' trail into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in the basin around 5,700 to 6,000 ft.

Note that FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the drive to this trailhead entirely.
hazards: Several parallel gullies and ledge systems on the south face that look identical and do not all go — the documented way to get cliffed out here
A reported truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully
Loose rock and rubble in the gully and on the summit ledges, with parties above you
Lookalike notches and false summits near the top
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the standard drive entirely

waysIn.name: Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake (Holden Village)
waysIn.notes: A longer alternate reaches the same basin from the east over Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake out of Holden Village. It is used by parties already doing that loop, not as a way in.
waysIn.whyThisWay: For parties already doing the Holden Village, Lyman Lake and Spider Gap loop who drop into Phelps Basin from the east; a much longer trip than walking up Phelps Creek.

name: East Face
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (~3,400 ft, reached via ~8.7 mi of Icicle Creek Road southwest of Leavenworth), follow the Stuart Lake Trail south along Mountaineer Creek. At about 2.5 miles, bear left (south) at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (this junction is also where the Lake Stuart fork continues straight); the trail crosses Mountaineer Creek on a log/boulder crossing that can be a wet, awkward ford in early season high water. Continue climbing through forest and over a boulder field to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly 4.3 miles from the trailhead — this is the last reliable, easily accessed water source and most parties treat water here before pushing on. Skirt the lake's west shore and its south end on climbers' trail through talus to the base of the infamous Aasgard Pass climb: an unmaintained, badly eroded boot-path that gains roughly 2,200-2,500 ft in well under a mile of steep, loose scree, boulders and (through at least June, sometimes into July) lingering snow/ice that can require an ice axe and even crampons or micro-spikes — this is the single biggest approach hazard and crux of the day, with real rockfall risk from parties above and easy route-finding mistakes in cloud or whiteout. Top out at Aasgard Pass (~7,750-7,800 ft), roughly 5 miles and ~4,400 ft above the trailhead. From the pass, work uphill to the south and southwest across talus and boulders toward the tower, then around beneath its east-facing aspect, staying high along the rim of the Enchantment basin; expect additional short snow patches and blocky talus underfoot right up to the base of the face, with no water beyond what you carried from Colchuck Lake or scooped from snowmelt trickles.
descent: Witches Tower's E/SE Face is a short route — one pitch of fourth-class climbing up the light-colored ("white rock") face to the small, exposed summit block — so full-rope-length rappelling is not mandatory, but many parties prefer not to reverse the exposed ledges. The commonly used descent is to downclimb/scramble off the South Face or Southwest Corner side (Class 2-4, the same terrain used as the standard walk-up/scramble route) back down to the notch/col southwest of the tower, then rejoin the Aasgard Pass approach for the hike out. Where climbers do rope up for the final step off the summit or down the face itself, expect a single ~100-150 ft rappel from natural gear — a slung horn, block, or tree rather than fixed bolts; a single 60m rope doubled (30m per strand) or even a 30m rope run single-strand is enough for this one rappel. Descent-specific hazards: exposed, sometimes loose/exfoliating granite on the upper face and summit block, fast-moving afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed summit with no quick retreat, and then the long, knee-jarring downclimb of Aasgard Pass's loose talus/scree back to Colchuck Lake, which many parties find harder and slower than the ascent, especially with residual snow/ice underfoot.
hazards: Looser, more blocky rock than the South Face/West Buttress lines
Possible lingering snow or low-angle ice (~WI2/M1) on the upper face into early summer
Little known and little traffic — route-finding is on you
A short, exposed slabby ledge near the summit carries real fall consequence despite the low technical grade (2006 first-hand account)

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass, then south and southwest to the light-coloured rock below Dragontail's south ridge
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the talus is clear; snow patches persist right up to the base into midsummer
waysIn.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, the Stuart Lake Trail to the signed fork at about 2.5 miles, left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and across Mountaineer Creek, then up through forest and a boulder field to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly 4.3 miles. Last reliable water.

Skirt the lake's west shore and its south end on climbers' trail through talus to the foot of Aasgard Pass, then up the eroded boot path — 2,200 to 2,500 ft in well under a mile of loose scree, boulders and lingering snow. This is the biggest hazard of the day and the place route-finding errors happen in cloud.

From the pass at roughly 7,750-7,800 ft, work uphill to the south and southwest across talus and boulders, staying high along the rim of the basin, to reach the tower's east-facing side.

No water above Colchuck Lake beyond snowmelt trickles.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: 2,200-2,500 ft of loose eroded scree, snow and ice into July, rockfall from parties above
Blocky talus and short snow patches right up to the base
Little or no protection on the climbing itself
A four-foot summit slot that must be jumped
The descent is normally down the south face or southwest corner, i.e. NOT the way you came — you finish on the other side of the tower
No water above Colchuck Lake

name: Southwest Ridge
approach: In 2026 FR-9737-112 is washed out and barricaded at the bottom, so walk its final mile-plus to the Beverly Creek Trailhead (at ~3,600 ft); from there, start on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391. After a short, mellow half mile paralleling Beverly Creek, bear right at the signed junction onto the Bean Creek Trail (#1391A), leaving the Turnpike Trail behind. The Bean Creek Trail climbs steadily through forest and then opens into Bean Creek Basin around the 2.5-mile mark — a broad, flower-choked meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats; this is the scenic highlight of the approach and a natural rest/water stop. Bean Creek itself is the last dependable water source. Its crossings are easy rock-hops by mid-to-late summer but can be swift, cold, and genuinely hazardous during May–June snowmelt, so plan accordingly if going early season. Beyond the basin the trail (tread becomes intermittent in the upper meadows) climbs switchbacks up to Earl Pass at roughly 6,200 ft — the broad saddle on the divide between the Bean Creek and Standup Creek drainages, about 3.5–4 miles and ~2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead. This pass has scattered flat tent sites and is the standard high camp for parties splitting the trip, or the pack-cache point for day-scramblers. From Earl Pass, leave the trail and pick up the boot path climbing the southwest ridge directly toward the summit. This final ~800 vertical feet is the crux of the trip: a sustained, unrelenting class 2 scramble on loose scree, sand, and broken rock with only an intermittent climbers' track — go slow, test holds, and be mindful of kicking rock onto anyone below. The ridge tops out on Earl Peak's 7,036-ft summit with a full panorama of the Stuart Range from Mt. Stuart to Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail.
descent: This is a walk-off — no rappelling is involved. Descend by reversing the ascent line: pick your way back down the loose, steep southwest ridge scree/sand to Earl Pass, using extra caution on the descent since loose rock and sandy scree are more prone to sliding underfoot going downhill, and stick to the established boot path where possible to limit erosion and rockfall onto other parties. From Earl Pass, rejoin and follow the Bean Creek Trail back down through Bean Creek Basin (re-crossing Bean Creek — again a hazard consideration in early-season high water) and the short connector back onto the Beverly Turnpike Trail to the Beverly Creek Trailhead. In poor visibility, the upper boot path across the open ridge can be hard to follow, so note landmarks (or track your ascent) on the way up. Some parties extend the day with an easy ridge traverse over to neighboring Bean Peak before dropping back to Earl Pass, but the standard descent is the straightforward reverse of the SW ridge/Bean Creek approach.
hazards: loose talus
early-season snow
afternoon heat

waysIn.name: Bean Creek Trail to Earl Pass
waysIn.season: Class 2 on dry ground from July into October, and a popular spring snow climb before that, when an axe and sometimes crampons are wanted on the steep south-facing summit slopes.
waysIn.notes: From the road-end trailhead start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed beside Beverly Creek, and at the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the wrong valley for this peak. The Bean Creek tread climbs through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley, drops to a ford of Bean Creek, then keeps climbing until the forest breaks open into a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. That basin is the last dependable water. At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than left into the upper basin; tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking to a broad saddle on the divide.
hazards: Bean Creek ford runs cold and pushy in May and June
Old avalanche debris crosses the trail just above the ford
Sustained loose scree, sand and broken rock on the final ridge that is easy to kick onto a party below
No dependable water above the meadows
Steep, icy south-facing snow on spring ascents
Afternoon heat on the exposed ridge

waysIn.name: Standup Creek trail
waysIn.notes: From the Standup Creek trailhead, the trail runs up a gentle valley, then steepens through open hillside to the southwest ridge of Earl Peak, where a boot path leads to the summit. Quieter and gentler at first than the Bean Creek side, with the hard climbing saved for the upper slopes.
hazards: Sustained loose scree, sand and broken rock on the final ridge that is easy to kick onto a party below
Steep, icy south-facing snow on spring ascents
Afternoon heat on the exposed ridge
Boot path on the upper southwest ridge; descent on loose sandy scree is more error-prone
waysIn.whyThisWay: For a quieter, gentler start from the Standup Creek side, or when making a loop that crosses the ridge between the two creeks, with the hard climbing saved for the upper slopes.

name: Standup Creek Route
approach: Access is via Standup Creek Road, reached from Stafford Creek Road off the Teanaway River Road near Cle Elum. The Standup Creek Trail #1369 follows an old road with little early elevation gain, crosses Standup Creek six to seven times, passes through brushy sections with some downed trees, then switchbacks up through forest and meadows to the ~6,200-ft saddle at the head of the drainage. The Labor Mountain Fire closure order on this trail has been lifted, as the Cle Elum Ranger District's trail crew reported on September 25, 2026; expect burned forest and downed trees in the drainage.
descent: Reverse the ridge scramble back to the ~6,200-ft saddle, then descend the Standup Creek Trail back through its creek crossings to the trailhead, or continue over the saddle onto the Bean Creek Trail to exit via Beverly Creek Trailhead if running a loop/shuttle.
hazards: Multiple creek crossings that can be difficult in high water or early season.
Brushy sections and downed trees on the lower trail.
Loose rock on the upper ridge and summit block.

name: East Face
approach: From the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616 (elev. ~2,850 ft), follow the Pete Lake Trail #1323 west and north through open, nearly-flat forest along Cooper River/Lemah Meadow terrain — easy tread and wildflower meadows for about 4 miles to the south shore of Pete Lake, a popular first camp and reliable water source. Continue past the lake about a mile, through Lemah Meadow, to the Pacific Crest Trail junction and turn north onto the PCT. After about a mile of PCT travel, watch for a wide avalanche path with heavy blowdown crossing the trail near the confluence of Chimney Creek — this is the turnoff for the climb. Leave the PCT and work climber's-right across the avalanche debris to pick up a boot/climber's path on the true-right side of Chimney Creek (it starts roughly 20 yards inside the timber at an obvious logjam that serves as the creek crossing, and is marked intermittently with orange flagging and cairns). The path crosses three brushy ravines, and pushes through alder and vine maple before breaking into open moraine and a hanging basin — cairns mark the line through this stretch, which is the main route-finding crux of the approach. A rock buttress called Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft), overlooking Chimney Creek's waterfalls, marks the top of the brush; most parties reach it in 4-5 hours from the trailhead. Sunrise Knob and flat-topped boulder sites with water in the basins at about 4,600-4,800 ft are the usual high camps (most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip); from camp the moraine leads up to the toe of the Chimney Glacier. Reliable water is at Pete Lake and the low Chimney Creek crossings; above the moraine plan on melting snow or glacier water. Hazards: the avalanche-path crossing (blowdown, lingering snow/avalanche debris into early summer), loose/brushy ravine crossings, and standard glacier travel hazards (crevasses, moats) gaining and crossing the Chimney Glacier to the base of the route.
descent: Reverse the ascent line rather than continuing over the summit block. From the summit, rappel the three summit pitches back to the broad ledge below the tower (two rappels on a single rope; some parties make three), then traverse back through the notch/gully between the main and south summits (a short reversal of the ascent gully, Class 3-4 downclimbing over loose debris or snow/ice depending on season). Where the rock steepens near the base of the face, on the wet, lower-angle slabs just above the glacier, most parties make two rappels over these fourth-class steps using a single rope (a 50-60m/165ft rope is enough for each); anchors here are natural — slung horns and blocks rather than bolts — so carry cord/webbing to back up or replace old tat, especially early in the season. Below the raps, a final short third-class downclimb regains the bergschrund/moat crossing back onto the Chimney Glacier, then reverse the moraine and climber's path to Sunrise Knob and the Pete Lake Trail. Watch for loose rock/rockfall in the gully, wet slick rock on the fourth-class rappel steps, and crevasse/moat hazard back on the glacier.
hazards: loose/choss rock in the entry gully and lower pitches — test every hold
rockfall
glacier travel with crevasses and a dynamic bergschrund/moat at the base of the face
exposed, committing low-5th-class chimney near the summit
remote location with slow potential rescue
long day; many parties plan 3 days (approach, climb, exit)

waysIn.name: Pete Lake trail and the PCT, then the Chimney Creek climbers' path to the moraine basin
waysIn.season: Early summer is better than late here. As the season runs on the glacier opens up and the moat at the foot of the rock becomes the thing that turns parties around
waysIn.notes: Start at the Pete Lake trailhead off Cooper Lake Road, FR 46 then FR 4616. Trailhead elevations are given from about 2,790 to 2,900 ft, so do not treat any one figure as exact. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Bikes are allowed on roughly the first two and a half miles of trail and no further. Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River, about four flat forested miles to Pete Lake, then on past the lake staying left at the forks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT roughly a mile to a mile and a half. The turn-off is a landmark, not a mileage, and parties consistently describe it the same way: the trail crosses an old avalanche swathe at about 3,360 ft and switchbacks sharply. Stop at that hairpin and look west across the valley. Twin waterfalls come down out of a hanging basin — that meltwater is coming off the Chimney Glacier and that basin is where you are going. To the right of the falls are two rounded rock outcrops and further right a cliff band; the climbers' path goes up the forest between the rounded outcrops and the cliff band. The path starts at an obvious logjam that gives a creek crossing, only about twenty yards inside the forest. Orange flagging appears in places and should not be relied on. One known wrong turn on that path: it climbs north-west and runs up to a rocky gully. Do not go up the rocky gully. The line continues left through vine maple and bracken fern, where the tread is buried under a season's growth. The path crosses three ravines, the second being the awkward one, and reaches bivy ground below the moraine. A rock buttress above the waterfalls is known as Sunrise Knob at roughly 4,650 to 4,700 ft; another party camped in a meadow at about 4,800 ft. Times from the car to that camp are reported anywhere from four and a half to over six hours, and planning three days is a common recommendation for what many parties attempt in two.
hazards: The moat and bergschrund at the base of the east face, which can be impassable late season
Crevasses on the Chimney Glacier and an active icefall between the lower and upper sections
Very serious route-finding — a well-known serious fall on this peak happened off route
Loose rock throughout the summit ledges and gullies
Vine maple and bracken burying the climbers' path, and flagging that may lead nowhere
Mosquitoes heavy down at lake level

name: West Ridge / Southwest Face
approach: From SR 20 near Newhalem, park at the Goodell Creek Group Campground (~600 ft) just east of Goodell Creek. The climbers' path starts behind a large boulder at the back of the campground and follows the old Goodell Creek roadbed upvalley for roughly 3.5-4 miles of gentle but brushy going (expect deadfall and a handful of washouts - this is an unmaintained boot path, not a maintained trail); two creek crossings low on the path can run high and fast on hot afternoons from snowmelt. An obvious cairn near 1,700 ft marks where the route leaves the roadbed and climbs steeply up a timbered spur ridge south of Terror Creek, passing about 3,200 ft on the way up. From there, benches of heather, slabs and rock lead up into Terror Basin (~5,800 ft, roughly 5,200 ft of gain and 6-7 miles in), the standard base camp for McMillan/Inspiration objectives, with reliable running water and flat tent sites. From camp, a long ascending traverse across snow, slabs and heather (crossing a shallow snow-fed depression near 5,500 ft) gains the Terror Glacier below West McMillan Spire - travel is often unroped in firm late-season conditions but crevasses can open, so assess conditions and carry basic glacier gear (axe, crampons).
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line. Downclimb the exposed 3rd-class summit ridge/block back to the West-East McMillan saddle - stay alert here, as the exposure is the route's main hazard on both ascent and descent. The short rock step just below the saddle (the 4th-class rib/ledge variant, or the head of the steep snow gully if snow has firmed up) is the crux of the descent; most parties make a single rappel here off a natural anchor (rock horn or sling/tat around a block - there is no fixed/bolted hardware on this route) rather than downclimb loose or steep terrain. A single 30-40 m rope is sufficient for this one rappel. From the base of the step, reverse the snow/glacier traverse back into Terror Basin camp, then follow the climbers' path back down the timbered ridge to the Goodell Creek trailhead, watching again for the low creek crossings running higher in the afternoon and for loose, eroded tread on the steep upper section.
hazards: loose rock, especially the reddish gully/ledge near the col
exposure on the ridge traverse and step-around moves
remoteness — no maintained trail, no cell coverage, long walk-out if injured
late-season moat/melt-out gap in the summit snow gully
habituated mountain goats at Terror Basin camp

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek to Terror Basin, then the Terror Glacier and the 40-degree snow gully to the West-East McMillan col
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From SR-20 near Newhalem, park at the Goodell Creek Group Campground at about 600 ft just east of Goodell Creek. The climbers' path starts behind a large boulder at the back of the campground and follows the old Goodell Creek roadbed upvalley for roughly 3.5-4 miles of gentle but brushy going, with deadfall and a handful of washouts. Two creek crossings low on the path can run high and fast on hot afternoons from snowmelt.

An obvious cairn near 1,700 ft marks where the route leaves the roadbed and climbs steeply up a timbered spur ridge south of Terror Creek, passing about 3,200 ft on the way up. Benches of heather, slabs and rock lead into Terror Basin at about 5,800 ft, roughly 5,200 ft of gain and 6-7 miles in, the standard base camp with reliable water and flat tent sites.

From camp, a long ascending traverse across snow, slabs and heather, crossing a shallow snow-fed depression near 5,500 ft, gains the Terror Glacier below West McMillan Spire.
hazards: Two creek crossings low on the path that run high and fast on hot afternoons
Deadfall and washouts on an unmaintained boot path
Crevasses can open on the Terror Glacier despite firm late-season travel being common
A snow gully steepening to about 40 degrees for its final 200-300 ft
Exposure on the summit ridge, the route's main hazard on both ascent and descent
Loose, eroded tread on the steep upper section of the path on the way out

name: East Ridge
approach: From Marblemount, drive Cascade River Road ~14.2 miles to the signed FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Road) junction and turn right. Cross the Cascade River on a concrete bridge and continue ~0.4 mile to a Y junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders — park here (roughly 1,150-1,300 ft; a long-standing washout on FR-1570 keeps most parties from driving any higher). A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every 50-150 ft leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth — about 1,700 vertical ft in the first mile — to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. At the saddle there is an easy-to-miss junction: go left and climb roughly 1,000 ft to Peak 5791, then traverse heather benches and meadows above Cyclone Lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of Snowking's East Ridge. Figure ~5 hours and ~5,000 ft of gain from the car to the Cyclone Lake/ridge base. In mid-June the climbers path was patchy from about 4,600 ft and the forest snow stayed firm even in the afternoon; the road needed medium clearance for stream crossings. In early July snow patches began near 5,100 ft and became continuous around the tarns by Cyclone Lake; running meltwater was available but dries once the snow is gone. The approach is a roller-coaster of small ups and downs over Found Peak and the ridge, so the day totals much more climbing than the summit height suggests, roughly 8,500-9,000 ft round trip.
descent: Reverse the East Ridge back to the Cyclone Lake basin, then retrace the flagged Kindy Ridge climbers' trail down to the FR-1570 parking area. In early season with good snow coverage, some parties glissade sections above Cyclone Lake; by late summer these slopes are bare talus and heather, so it's a walk-down.
hazards: Route-finding on the flagged climbers' trail, especially in fog or flat light
Loose, exposed rock if you drift onto the Class 3 southeast variant of the ridge
Lingering snow/cornices near the summit block into early summer
Washed-out FR-1570 adds significant extra approach mileage and elevation gain versus older trip reports

waysIn.name: The Kindy Creek roadbed and the ribbon-marked climbers' trail to the Point 5116 saddle
waysIn.season: June through September
waysIn.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles to the signed forest road 1570 junction and turn right. Cross the river on a concrete bridge and continue about half a mile to a Y-junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders; park there, at roughly 1,150 to 1,300 ft, because a long-standing washout keeps most parties from driving higher.

A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every fifty to a hundred and fifty feet leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth - about seventeen hundred vertical feet in its first mile, with few switchbacks - to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. From the saddle the route climbs roughly a thousand feet to Peak 5791, then traverses heather benches and meadows above the lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of the east ridge.
hazards: a rooty, eroded and very slick steep mile that is worse descending than ascending
an easy-to-miss junction at the saddle where the two routes on this peak diverge
no water on the steep climb from the roadbed
rolling ridge travel that takes longer than the distance suggests
an exposed camp and no bail-out once out on the ridge

waysIn.name: Camping at the lake below the ridge
waysIn.season: Same window
waysIn.notes: The lake below the ridge is the common overnight for this route and turns it from a very long day into a comfortable two. The camping is in the meadows on the lake's east side and there is reliable water. Parties doing it in a day still pass through the same ground and should treat the lake as the last water before the ridge.
hazards: no water above the lake
a wind-exposed basin camp
loose blocks where the ridge rises out of the benches
committing ridge travel with no easy descent off either side
waysIn.whyThisWay: When splitting the climb over two days, with a comfortable camp and reliable water in the lake meadows below the ridge.

name: East Ridge
approach: Start from the Cedar Creek trailhead near Mazama -- a different trailhead than the Silver Star Creek/Highway 20 pullout used for the Glacier and NE Ridge routes -- and gain the ridge near the confluence of Cedar and Early Winters Creeks, then follow the crest north and west for roughly 3.5 miles to the summit.
descent: From the summit, rope down or downclimb a short distance to gain the Silver Star Glacier, then descend the glacier west/northwest toward Burgundy Col. From the col, climb/hike up and over to the Burgundy Col climbers' trail, which drops back to Highway 20 near milepost 166 (roughly 4 miles from Washington Pass) — several miles of highway from the Cedar Creek Trailhead used for the approach. Carry glacier travel gear (and an ice axe/crampons in early season) for this descent, since it crosses real crevassed glacier terrain, not just snow slopes.
hazards: Loose, sometimes rotten rock typical of North Cascades alpine ridges.
Sustained, committing position along the ridge with limited retreat options.

waysIn.name: Cedar Creek Trailhead near Mazama, gaining the ridge at the Cedar and Early Winters Creek confluence
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: This is the route's defining logistical fact: it uses a different trailhead from every other route on the peak. Start from the Cedar Creek trailhead near Mazama, at the end of Sandy Butte-Cedar Creek Road #200 about 4.25 miles west of Mazama off SR-20, not the Silver Star Creek or Wine Spires pullouts on SR-20 that serve the Glacier and Northeast Ridge routes. Gain the ridge near the confluence of Cedar and Early Winters Creeks, then follow the crest north and west for roughly 3.5 miles to the summit. And note this is Silver Star Mountain in Okanogan County at 8,876 ft above Washington Pass, not the Silver Star Mountain in Clark County near Vancouver, Washington, which is a different peak entirely.
hazards: A descent that finishes at a different trailhead several highway miles from the start
Real crevassed glacier terrain on the descent
A 3.5-mile ridge traverse with sustained route-finding
Two peaks in Washington named Silver Star Mountain; this is the Okanogan County one

name: East Slope
approach: Start at the Thunder Creek Trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20 (turn in just past milepost 130). Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly 6-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp, then continue about half a mile and leave the maintained trail, dropping steeply to cross Thunder Creek, to climb the climbers' path up 'Lucky Ridge' to a bivy near the northeast corner of the lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier (~6,000 ft). Expect about 8 1/4 miles and 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead to this camp, roughly 9 hours with an overnight pack. Note: the footbridge that once crossed Thunder Creek near McAllister Camp is gone, so the crossing is a log jam or a wade — check current park trail conditions before you go.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the East Ridge back to Lucky Pass and descend the same eastern-margin line on the Borealis Glacier used on the ascent, staying off the central icefall. There is no established rappel line; parties without a rope can generally walk this off in good conditions, but carry a rope/pickets in case of deteriorating snow bridges.
hazards: Central icefall on the Borealis Glacier — stay on the climber's-right/eastern margin
Hidden crevasses, worse and more exposed by late September
Loose rock on the Class 3 East Ridge finish
Thunder Creek crossing can be difficult if the trail bridge is out
Long, remote approach with little to no cell coverage

waysIn.name: Thunder Creek and Lucky Ridge to the Borealis Glacier and Lucky Pass
waysIn.season: Mid-July through August, while enough of the Borealis Glacier's snowpack remains to bridge crevasses; by late September the glacier is largely bare and the pass can be bullet ice and loose rock
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Thunder Creek trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130, near 1,200 ft. Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly six miles to McAllister Camp, then continue about half a mile farther.

A ford of Thunder Creek at a log jam is normally required and the footbridge that once crossed near McAllister Camp is gone — check current park conditions rather than assuming a dry crossing.

Leave the maintained trail there, cross Thunder Creek, and climb the climbers' path up Lucky Ridge, the ridge between McAllister and Thunder creeks: roughly 4,000 ft of gain over a couple of miles through brush and devil's club, with two short cliff-band scrambles. Camp near the northeast corner of the proglacial lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier around 6,000 ft, with the icefall in view above.

Rope up around 7,000 ft on the flat snow shelf and climb the glacier's eastern margin — the central icefall splits the lower and upper tiers and has caught parties who drifted climber's-left.
hazards: A mandatory Thunder Creek ford with a powerful current, worse later in the day as snowmelt rises
The central icefall on the Borealis Glacier — stay on the eastern margin
Hidden crevasses that open both vertically and horizontally, and moats where snow pulls off rock, worst late season
Cloud and fog that move in on this glacier routinely
A long, remote approach with no cell coverage

name: East Wilmans Spire
approach: From Granite Falls, drive the paved Mountain Loop Highway east roughly 31 miles (passing the Verlot Public Service Center) to Barlow Pass, where pavement ends and the Monte Cristo Road is gated to motor vehicles. Hike or mountain-bike the flat, gated road about 4 miles along the South Fork Sauk River to the historic Monte Cristo townsite (a washout near the Twin Bridges area may require a ford or log crossing of the river). From the townsite, pick up the Glacier Basin Trail and follow it a short distance before leaving the trail to climb a steep talus/scree gully - snow-covered and firmer in early season, loose and increasingly rockfall-prone once melted out by mid/late summer - up to the east notch/col below East Wilmans Spire, where the roped climbing begins.
descent:
From the summit, make two single-rope rappels down the line of ascent. The first is short, off the three-piton anchor on the summit block, and lands at the slung rock at the top of pitch 2; the second takes you down pitch 2 to the top of pitch 1.

From there most parties do not rappel again: they climb back over the 20-ft 5.5 crack that pitch 1 downclimbs on the way in, then downclimb to the east notch. That reversal is made unroped with about a thousand feet of exposure below and is the most committing move of the descent, though it goes more easily backwards than it looks. Some parties instead make a third rappel straight down into the gully from the top of pitch 1, which is why recorded rappel counts here differ between two and three.

From the notch, downclimb the approach gully — glissading remaining snow where present, or picking carefully through loose talus and scree later in the season — back to the Glacier Basin Trail, then retrace the approach through Monte Cristo townsite to Barlow Pass.
hazards: The route's volcanic breccia rock is loose in places, particularly on east-facing sections and low on pitches.
The approach gully sheds rockfall once it melts out of snow, typically by mid/late July.
Late-season talus/scree in the gully is loose and unpleasant, increasing slip and rockfall risk.
The summit is very small and exposed on all sides.

waysIn.name: Glacier Basin Trail to the east notch
waysIn.season: Jun-mid Jul, on snow
waysIn.notes: Reach the Monte Cristo townsite on foot or by bike from Barlow Pass, then take the Glacier Basin Trail less than a mile. The spire stands above the trail, roughly 2,000 ft above the basin. When it makes sense, leave the trail and start up toward the base of the ridge — a snowfield early in the season, extremely loose talus once it has gone. Snow or talus leads up a narrowing gully to the lower col, steepening as it goes, commonly 35 to 45 degrees, with the final couloir steeper and more exposed than anything below it. Best done early in the year while the gully still holds snow: melted out it is loose scree badly exposed to rockfall and a poor outing in late summer. Fixed stations exist in the gully and parties have used them to bypass melted-out gaps on the way down.
hazards: Serious rockfall in the approach gully once the snow has melted out
Steep, exposed snow in the final couloir — crampons, and a second tool is worth having
Cornices and hanging snow slabs above the left-hand branch of the gully
Moats and a schrund where the gully snow melts back from the rock
Loose rock on the route itself, especially low on each pitch and on the east aspect

name: East Ridge (Inspiration Glacier)
approach: Start at the Eldorado Trailhead (Eldorado Creek Climbers' Path) at mile 20 of Cascade River Road, elevation ~2,100 ft (pit toilet at the parking area). From the parking area, backtrack downstream about 90 feet on the road and look for a log or a clump of three trees spanning the Cascade River — cross here (this crossing can be exposed and slick when wet or in high water; a rope/handline is prudent for less experienced parties), then walk roughly 100 feet perpendicular to the river to pick up the climbers' trail. The path climbs steeply through heavy timber, gaining about 1,500 ft before breaking out onto talus. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulder field, staying climber's right to avoid an unnecessary crossing of Eldorado Creek, until the talus eases into the open, beautiful alpine Eldorado Creek Basin (a common first camp at roughly 5,400–5,600 ft, ~3 miles and 3,300 ft from the trailhead). From the basin, climb up onto a rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft, then drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (an alternate/second camp at 6,100–6,400 ft, with reliable running water). From Roush Basin, ascend broken talus and slabs onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and continue up moderate glacier slopes to a high camp near 7,500–7,800 ft on the Eldorado–Inspiration Glacier saddle, with views of Moraine Lake, McAllister Glacier and Klawatti Glacier. Rope up for glacier travel here — the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers carry real crevasse hazard, worse as the day warms; parties have broken through hidden snow-bridged creek channels even in the lower basins in spring. From high camp, cross the mostly flat Inspiration Glacier aiming for the low gap on Eldorado's lower East Ridge, then follow the ridge/snow arete up to the base of the summit knife-edge. Total gain is roughly 6,700–6,800 ft trailhead-to-summit; guided parties budget 5–7 hours to high camp and another 3–5 hours (6–9 hours total on summit day) from camp to the top.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the exposed, corniced knife-edge summit ridge (in certain conditions a very thin edge with steep — 40–45°+ — flanks; ice axe and crampons essentially mandatory, and rope/running-belay technique is common for less experienced members), continue down through the gap in the lower East Ridge, then rope up again to cross the Inspiration Glacier and descend the Eldorado Glacier back to Roush Basin, over the intervening ridge into Eldorado Creek Basin, and down the boulder field and timbered climbers' trail to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappels are used on the standard route; multiple trip reports and guide-service itineraries describe the descent purely in terms of downclimbing and reversing glacier travel, and note that some parties have even skied the ridge and glaciers in spring conditions rather than roping for rappels. Watch for softening snow bridges and increasing crevasse hazard on the glaciers later in the day (afternoon descents in summer are notably less secure than an early-morning ascent), and for the knife-edge becoming icy/firm late-season, which can make the downclimb more consequential and prompt some parties to belay short sections rather than rappel them.
hazards: crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier
the exposed knife-edge summit arête
whiteout navigation on the broad glacier
soft snow on the arête on warm afternoons
difficult Cascade River crossing near the trailhead at high water/early season
glide cracks forming on the lower glacier slabs by mid-summer
no reliable water above the boulder field — winter-camping skills needed at high camp

A bergschrund crossing sits at roughly 8200ft on the East Ridge glacier approach; reported as easily navigable in normal late-summer conditions, but check current beta as crevasse/bergschrund opening varies season to season

waysIn.name: Eldorado Creek climbers' path to Inspiration Glacier high camp
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, once the talus is bare
waysIn.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount roughly 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area at about 2,100 ft. The first ten miles are paved; the rest is gravel and washboard.

The path does not leave from the parking area. Walk back down the road about 90 feet and look for the log (historically a large single log, sometimes a clump of trees) spanning the Cascade River. The crossing shifts year to year and is slick when wet — a handline is worth carrying for a party that is not confident on a log. On the far bank walk perpendicular to the river roughly 100 feet to pick up the boot path.

The path climbs steeply and relentlessly through old-growth timber with no water, gaining about 1,500 ft before it breaks out into the boulder field. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulders, staying climber's right so you do not cross Eldorado Creek unnecessarily. The boulder field is universally described as the worst part of the trip, and worse on the way down with a heavy pack.

Above the boulders the ground eases into Eldorado Creek Basin (roughly 5,400-5,600 ft, about 3 miles and 3,300 ft from the car), a common first camp. To continue, climb onto the rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft and drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (6,100-6,400 ft, running water). From Roush, broken talus and slabs lead onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier; rope up here. Moderate glacier slopes lead to high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle around 7,500-7,800 ft.

Overnight stays need a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. Eldorado is a high-use cross-country zone; there is an advance lottery and reservations on Recreation.gov, but permits for the areas off Cascade River Road (Eldorado, Boston Basin, Cascade Pass) must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
hazards: Cascade River log crossing — slick when wet, position shifts year to year
Boulder field is the crux of the walk, worse descending under a heavy pack
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers, worsening as the day warms
Featureless flat glacier — whiteout navigation to The Gap
Exposed summit knife-edge; crevasses on the ridge crest itself

waysIn.name: Late-spring snow cover (skis or boots)
waysIn.season: late May-June
waysIn.notes:
In late spring the upper approach is continuous snow and the boulder field problem largely disappears, which is why many parties prefer this window. It does not make the whole approach snow: a late-May park report described the route as snow-free until just before Eldorado Basin was gained around 5,000 ft, with the boulder fields completely melted out — so expect a dry, steep forest climb first and snow only above.

Ski parties commonly carry ski boots and walk the forest section in approach or running shoes, switching over at snow line.

The trade is avalanche exposure. Large avalanches sweep parts of this route in winter and spring, and Cascade River Road itself can be buried by avalanche debris miles below the trailhead in a heavy year, adding road miles before you even start.
hazards: Avalanche paths across the approach and the road in spring
Snow-bridged creek channels in the lower basins — parties have punched through
Road may be closed or buried well below the trailhead
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late May and June, when snow covers the upper approach and the boulder field, and parties accept avalanche exposure for faster ground; ski parties also choose it for the descent.

name: Northwest Couloir / Eldorado Glacier
approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado Trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 (~2,100 ft), cross the Cascade River via the log/three-tree crossing about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, then climb the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield (roughly to 4,500 ft) and on into Eldorado Creek Basin. From there, continue as for the East Ridge over the Roush Divide and up the Eldorado Glacier, then trend toward the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col on the mountain's northwest side to reach the wild Marble Creek Cirque, with views of Dorado Needle and Early Morning Spire. The approach to this face is longer and more involved than the East Ridge approach — a long, somewhat complicated route across glaciated and crevassed terrain, so rope up for the glacier sections. High camp is typically established either in Eldorado Creek/Roush Creek Basin or higher at the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier site (~7,500–7,600 ft). One recorded ascent (climbing from the trailhead in a single push) took roughly 5 hours to reach the couloir's base; that party also used a shortcut of a belayed downclimb (~35 m) and two 30-meter rappels down a snow/rock gully near the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col to drop directly to within about 100 yards of the couloir, which meaningfully shortens the standard glacier traverse but is a variation, not the only way in — most parties simply continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft. Hazards on approach: crevasses on the Eldorado/Inspiration Glaciers, a long featureless glacier crossing that can be disorienting in whiteout, and the optional gully downclimb/rappel shortcut is itself exposed snow-and-rock terrain.
descent: From the summit, do not reverse the couloir — descend via the standard East Ridge / Inspiration Glacier route: downclimb the knife-edge summit ridge, drop through the gap in the lower East Ridge, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, then descend the Eldorado Glacier back toward Roush Basin and Eldorado Creek Basin, finishing on the timbered climbers' trail back to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead (see the East Ridge route for full detail). This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappels required on the descent itself — one party even skied the knife-edge ridge and glacier on the way down. Rappelling comes up on this route only on the approach/entry into the couloir, not on the summit descent: one party used a 40-meter rappel off the Inspiration Glacier side to drop into the couloir's gully system, anchored on two pitons with some newish tat, and noted a full 60m rope would get a party through everything in one rappel rather than needing to downclimb the remainder — but again, this is describing getting into the route, not descending from the summit. Because the descent is the shared East Ridge walk-off, treat glacier crevasse hazard and knife-edge icing exactly as on that route, and carry a rope for the glacier crossings regardless of whether any rappelling was used higher on the mountain.
hazards: crevasses on the glacier
steep snow and short ice steps
the exposed summit arête
avalanche on the approach early season
rockfall/icefall funneling down the couloir — described by climbers as 'an extreme funnel'
cornices and crevasses at the couloir's exit near the knife-edge ridge
crevasse crossings on the long Inspiration/Marble Creek Glacier traverse approach

waysIn.name: Rappel off the ice cap into the Marble Creek cirque, then the couloir splitting the northwest face
waysIn.season: Highly conditions-dependent. Spring, roughly April to early May, can give steep thin ice and moderate mixed; mid-to-late summer the couloir is usually mostly snow with a few ice steps; a good cold snap in late October or November can bring in firm, well-bonded ice. Grade moves with it, roughly AI2-3 up to WI3 in lean conditions
waysIn.notes:
Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 near 2,100 ft, the log crossing of the Cascade River about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield around 4,500 ft, and on into Eldorado Creek Basin.

From there, continue as for the East Ridge over the Roush Divide and up the Eldorado Glacier, then trend toward the mountain's northwest side and the wild Marble Creek Cirque. High camp is either in Eldorado Creek / Roush Creek Basin or at the Eldorado-Inspiration site near 7,500-7,600 ft.

The usual way in is from above: follow the East Ridge glacier track to about 8,100 ft, traverse to the notch between the North Ridge and the first rock spire — the same notch sometimes called the Eldorado-Dean's Spire or Dean's Tower col — and rappel from it into the cirque below. A full 60 m rope gets a party through in one; parties on shorter ropes have downclimbed the remainder. One party used a belayed downclimb of about 35 m plus two 30 m rappels to land within about 100 yards of the couloir. One single-push ascent took roughly five hours from the trailhead to the couloir's base.

The alternative is simply to continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft.
hazards: An extreme funnel: the whole face feeds into a narrow confined couloir, so anything the leader dislodges lands on the belay
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers and a long featureless crossing that is disorienting in whiteout
A moat or bergschrund where the glacier meets the couloir, widening through the summer
Cornices and crevasses at the couloir's exit near the knife-edge ridge
Rappelling the couloir is the only retreat once you are high, and it is slow — the practical escape is over the top

name: West Arete
approach: Start at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road, follow the climbers' trail up Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin, camp near the base of the East Ridge (about 7,500 ft), then cross the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers to Dorado Needle Col and make a loose fourth-class downclimb into the Marble Creek cirque, traversing to the toe of the arete near 6,000 ft. Typically a 3-day trip (approach day, climb day, exit day); the first roughly 800 ft of climbing is Class 4 before harder 5th-class sections.
descent: From the summit, descend the East Ridge — most parties find this significantly easier and more straightforward than downclimbing the loose West Arete — then return to camp via the Inspiration/Eldorado Glacier.
hazards: Rockfall/loose-rock hazard along the full length of the arête.
Long, remote, multi-day approach with significant weather exposure.
Possible unplanned bivouac if the party is slow through the confusing middle section.

The approach traverses the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers to reach the foot of the arête, and those crevasses open through the summer — by late season the traverse is genuinely more complex than the climbing grade suggests. Roped glacier travel and crevasse rescue are needed before the rock starts.

waysIn.name: Over the ice cap to Dorado Needle Col, then down into Marble Creek Cirque
waysIn.season: Mid to late summer once fully snow-free, with maximum daylight for a long climbing day; Cascade River Road is often not open until late June
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road, follow the climbers' trail up Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin, and gain the Eldorado Glacier. Most parties treat this as three days: approach, climb, exit, with a base camp at the East Ridge site near 7,500 ft or on the western margin of the Eldorado Glacier.

The defining feature of the approach is that you must get down to the base. The line runs from the ice cap across to the Dorado Needle Col area, then a loose fourth-class downclimb — accounts on the neighbouring line describe rappelling, steep névé downclimbing and moat work over roughly 1,000 ft of descent — into the Marble Creek Cirque on Eldorado's west side, and the toe of the ridge is at the bottom of that.

This is a long day: parties have taken up to about 17 hours round trip from the East Ridge base camp, and an unplanned bivouac is a real possibility if the middle section goes slowly.

A warning from parties who have done it: published route descriptions for this arête have been called inaccurate and sandbagged, and at least one party went off route immediately as a result. Trust the terrain over the topo.
hazards: A loose fourth-class downclimb into the cirque that has to be reversed or bypassed at the end of the day
Rockfall and loose rock over the full length of the arête, including the opening pitch
Large moats on both sides of the ridge at its foot, and a building-sized snow remnant to keep clear of
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers that open through the summer
A confusing middle section where slow progress turns into a bivouac

name: Elephant Butte Standard Route (Stetattle/Sourdough Ridge)
approach: Drive State Route 20 (North Cascades Highway) to milepost 126 and turn off at the sign for the village of Diablo, a Seattle City Light company town. Park near the river across from the domed swimming pool; the Sourdough Mountain Trail begins immediately behind the pool building (roughly 890-900 ft). Follow the trail as it switchbacks steeply through forest. At an unmarked junction around 4,300-4,400 ft, leave the maintained trail and head up onto the open crest of Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge (roughly 6,500 ft) rather than continuing to the Sourdough Mountain Lookout; if you reach the Sourdough Creek crossing and open views of Diablo Lake, you have gone past the turn-off. From the ridge crest, continue along the mostly open, trail-less ridge toward Elephant Butte.
descent: From the summit, retrace the approach: regain the ridge crest above the Elephant Butte bypass terrain, then follow the open ridge back toward the Sourdough Mountain Trail junction (around 6,500 ft, then the junction at 4,300-4,400 ft). Drop onto the maintained trail and switchback down through forest to the trailhead at Diablo. Parties using this as a through-route to the Southern Pickets instead continue along the ridge system toward Pioneer Ridge/McMillan Creek and the Pickets rather than returning to Diablo.
hazards: Loose, exposed class 3 rock on the ridge and near Elephant Butte
Steep brushy/mossy terrain with poor footing on the bypass around the peak
Early- and late-season snowfields on the ridge crest
Very long, remote approach far from any maintained trail or quick rescue access

waysIn.name: Sourdough Mountain Trail to the Stetattle Ridge crest
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the Diablo trailhead behind the pool building, climb the Sourdough Mountain Trail's switchbacks. The Sourdough Creek crossing lies beyond the turn-off on the way to the lookout, so reaching it means you have gone too far. The turn-off is an unmarked junction somewhere around 4,300 to 4,400 ft — it is given variously between 4,000 and 4,400 ft, so treat the elevation as approximate and the feature as the thing to find. From it, a left turn takes you straight north up the ridge crest immediately west of Sourdough Creek rather than continuing toward the Sourdough Mountain lookout. You break out of the trees just before reaching the crest, at around 6,000 ft. On the ridge, keep on or southwest of the top: the northeast side is very steep.
hazards: The unmarked turn-off is easy to walk past; reaching the Sourdough Creek crossing means you have missed it
The northeast side of Stetattle Ridge drops away steeply the length of the walk
Brush, mossy micro-cliffs and steep impassable treed slopes on the ground around the summit obstacle
A long committing ridge walk with a large drop to Elephant Butte's base

name: Ellen Pea
approach: M&M Wall, also known as Supercave Wall for the tennis-court-sized cave crossing the cliff at mid-height, is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass. Park at a pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns below Washington Pass. From the highway, head directly uphill (west, away from the creek) toward the talus at the base of the Supercave gully, following it up and briefly left before rejoining the gully; it takes roughly 1 hour to reach the lower ledge and about 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the upper ledge and base of the longer routes.
descent: Descend via rappel using two ropes; expect some diagonal-rappel maneuvering to stay on anchors, or traverse off to a 3rd-class ramp partway down. Figure roughly an hour from the summit/top of the route back to the base.
hazards: Loose talus/creekbed terrain on the approach.
Water/seepage on lower pitches persists into early summer in wet years.
Full south-facing sun exposure with no shade until the cave.

waysIn.name: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
waysIn.season: Late June to September, once the gully has melted out and the lower pitches have dried; the highway over the pass is gated shut all winter, so there is no cold-season access at all.
waysIn.notes: Park at the roadside pullout near milepost 166 and start straight uphill to the west, away from the creek — there is no trail and no sign. Head for the talus at the foot of the gully that splits the wall; the gully forces you briefly out to the left before you rejoin it higher. Two ledge systems break the wall. The lower one comes first; keep going past it to the upper ledge, where the long routes start. The wall faces due south and there is no shade below the cave, so on a hot day the approach is the hottest part of the route.
hazards: Loose talus and creek-bed footing in the approach gully, with rockfall from anyone above you in it
Full south-facing sun on the whole approach with no shade until the cave
Water and seepage on the lower pitches persists into early summer in wet years
The highway is gated closed through winter and well into spring, so the approach can be unreachable by car

name: Southeast Ridge
approach: Start at the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead (~3,940 ft) at the end of Forest Road 5606, off Entiat River Road. Take the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437, which follows the North Fork Entiat River upstream through burned/downed timber from past wildfires — expect deadfall requiring detours over, under, or around logs in the lower miles, and a river/creek crossing (Grouse Creek, via a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail crossing, or a deteriorating footbridge depending on year and washout status) a few miles in. The trail climbs gently through forest, passing the Fern Lake Trail (#1436) junction at about mile 6.1 (roughly 1,300 ft of gain from the trailhead). Continue upvalley; around mile 7 the North Fork Entiat trail turns sharply east/right and switchbacks about a half mile up to its end at the junction with the Pyramid Mountain Trail (#1433) near 6,600 ft. Above this point the maintained trail effectively ends and the route goes cross-country: leave the trail here (or slightly before, depending on snow cover — the tread can be hard to follow once patchy snow sets in above ~4,800 ft in early season) and angle west/southwest, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald Peak. A good camp/staging flat sits around 7,000–7,100 ft in the open basin below Cardinal's north-middle saddle, convenient for both Emerald and neighboring Cardinal/Saska. From this basin, drop 200–300 ft to skirt cliff bands, then regain a 6,900 ft basin south of Emerald Peak. Cross a shoulder near 7,100 ft and climb a gully into the upper basin wedged between Saska and Emerald, which feeds the southeast side of Emerald's summit ridge — this is the start of the southeast ridge scramble proper. Water is reliably available along the North Fork Entiat River and its tributaries for the first ~7 miles but is scarce above the basin, so tank up before leaving the valley bottom. Total one-way distance to the base of the climbing is roughly 9–10 miles with about 3,200–3,400 ft of the route's total gain covered by the time you reach the upper basin, leaving a shorter, steeper final push to the ridge and summit.
descent: Descend by reversing the southeast ridge/gully line used on ascent: downclimb class 2–3 terrain from the summit block back to the notch in the upper basin between Saska and Emerald, then follow the gully back down to the 6,900 ft basin and re-cross the shoulder to the camp flat near 7,000–7,100 ft. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no fixed anchors or rappel stations are reported on this route, and parties climbing the Saska–Emerald–Cardinal group describe simul-downclimbing or careful scrambling rather than rappelling, since the class 2-3 terrain generally isn't steep or exposed enough to require rope work. The main descent hazards are loose, blocky rock in the gully (rockfall risk onto parties below, and ankle-turning talus/scree lower down) and, in early season, moderate snow in the gully requiring an ice axe and possibly crampons — parties have noted lingering snow patches into summer. From the basin, retrace the cross-country line back to the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction and descend the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 the full ~9 miles back to the trailhead, watching footing on the same deadfall and creek crossings encountered on the way in (a crampon-related slip near the final miles has been reported, so stay attentive even on the "easy" trail portion when fatigued). If any party member is uncomfortable with the exposure in the gully/notch section, a short hand-line or single rappel off natural gear (block/horn) could reasonably be rigged, but this is not standard practice for the route.
hazards: loose rock/choss in the summit gullies
routefinding among several similar gully/bench variations on the broad southeast side
remote approach — no cell service and hours from help
unmaintained, log-choked trail sections from past wildfire damage
lingering snow and possible cornices in the summit gullies through June
afternoon thunderstorms and wildfire smoke common in July-September

waysIn.name: North Fork Entiat to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the basin between Saska and Emerald
waysIn.season: Mid-Jul-Sep for snow-free scrambling; late May and June need an axe and crampons for neve in the summit gullies. October is popular for larch colour and brings short days
waysIn.notes:
From the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead near 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, take Trail #1437 upstream on a gentle grade — only about 1,300 ft of gain over six miles. The lower miles run through old burn and blowdown, so plan on working over and around deadfall rather than walking clean tread. Grouse Creek has been crossed on a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail crossing, or on a deteriorating footbridge, depending on the year.

Bear right at the Fern Lake fork and stay on #1437. Around mile 7 the trail swings sharply east and switchbacks half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction. In early season the tread gets hard to follow once snow patches start above roughly 4,800 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the junction and head west; the timber opens into a clearing within about a quarter mile. Fill and treat water there — the valley bottom is the last easy water and there is little of it above.

From the clearing the travel is cross-country: angle west then south-west, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald. Expect to give back 200-300 ft to skirt cliff bands before regaining the open basin floor around 6,900 ft. A camp flat sits near 7,000-7,100 ft.
hazards: Unmaintained, log-choked trail sections from past wildfire damage on the lower six miles
Grouse Creek crossing by logjam
Loose rock and choss in the summit gullies; several similar gully and bench variations do not all go
Steeply inclined south slab on the small summit whose slip line runs down the east face
Lingering snow and possible cornices in the summit gullies through June
Dry approach, last easy water a quarter mile past the trail's end
Remote, no cell service

waysIn.name: Emerald Park and Milham Pass from Lucerne
waysIn.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail and fork onto the Emerald Park trail, climbing along Emerald Park Creek to the Emerald Park meadows. Continue about two miles to Milham Pass and drop into the basin between Emerald and Saska, where the ridge begins. It depends on the boat schedule, but it is the natural choice when coming from the Lake Chelan side or linking peaks along the crest.
hazards: Approach trails sit inside a wildfire closure area; closure status must be checked
Boat-dependent access from Lake Chelan
Loose rock and choss in the summit gullies; several similar gully and bench variations do not all go
Steeply inclined south slab on the small summit whose slip line runs down the east face
Lingering snow and possible cornices in the summit gullies through June
Tarns in the high basin unreliable by mid-August; fully exposed to weather from the west
Remote, no cell service
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming from the Lake Chelan side or linking peaks along the crest; it needs the boat to Lucerne and a long walk up Emerald Park to Milham Pass, and the trail may be closed.

name: West Route
approach: Primary approach: from Entiat, drive Entiat River Road ~32.5 miles to Forest Road 5606, then ~3 switchbacking miles to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (~3,940 ft); hike NF Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley and leave the trail to gain the west-side gully below Emerald's summit block. Alternate approach: from Lucerne on Lake Chelan (reached by boat/ferry), hike the Emerald Park Trail #1230 up into Emerald Park and approach the peak's west side from there. In mid-June the North Fork Entiat trail had many fallen trees, the first three to four miles run through burned forest with little shade, and snow patches covered the trail from about 6,600 to 6,900 ft. By early July the trail had been cleared of most blowdowns, though a few logs still needed climbing over, and the basin below the peak had plenty of water and no snow crossings.
descent: Downclimb from the summit block back through the class 3 gully on the west side, taking care on the steep slab near the south summit and the East Face exposure; regain the basin and retrace either the North Fork Entiat or Emerald Park Trail approach.
hazards: Rockfall/loose rock in the erosion-carved gully
Exposure on the south summit's slab toward the East Face
Remote approach with minimal cell coverage

waysIn.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
waysIn.season: Mid-July into early October. Snow can hold in the gullies well into the season, and an axe is worth carrying early and mid-season.
waysIn.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. The base-finding below is written for this trail camp side.
hazards: Deep loose scree with a dug-in boot path; kicked rock runs onto parties below, so spread out and wear a helmet
Several gullies, correct one hidden until you round a buttress
Small summit area becomes exposed within a few paces of its centre
South point is a steeply inclined slab; a slip runs down the East Face
Nearby sub-summits are convincing and have been tagged by mistake
No water beyond the meadow
Remote, minimal cell coverage

waysIn.name: Emerald Park trail from Lucerne
waysIn.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail to the Emerald Park trail, and climb up Emerald Park to Milham Pass, which drops into the basin between Emerald and Saska. A boat-dependent alternative to the Entiat side, and the natural choice when coming from Lake Chelan. It reaches the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement. Where this line joins the climbing is unclear.
hazards: Approach trails affected by a wildfire closure; check status before going
Boat-dependent access from Lake Chelan
Rockfall and loose rock in the erosion-carved west gully
Exposure on the south summit slab toward the East Face
Basin tarns unreliable by mid-August; camp fully exposed to weather from the west
Remote, minimal cell coverage
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming from the Lake Chelan side by boat, or linking Emerald with Saska or other Chelan-side peaks, since it avoids the long drive and walk up the North Fork Entiat.

name: East Ridge (Prusik Pass)
approach: Reach Prusik Pass either from the west (Stuart Lake TH -> Colchuck Lake -> Aasgard Pass -> across the core Enchantment basin) or from the north/east via the longer Snow Creek/Snow Lakes trail (FST 1553) and the upper basin. From Prusik Pass, head west onto Enchantment Peak's east ridge.
descent: Downclimb the short 3rd-class step off the summit block carefully, then walk the ridge's minor humps back east to Prusik Pass. From there, descend the same way you came in — either back over Aasgard Pass to Colchuck Lake, or out via the Snow Lakes trail if approached from that side.
hazards: Exposure on the final ~15 ft summit-block scramble
Loose rock along the ridge
No reliable cell coverage

waysIn.name: Prusik Pass to the northeast summit
