waysIn.season: Late Jun to early Oct for snow-free ground; outside that the basin travel needs snowshoes or skis
waysIn.notes:
Prusik Pass is reached either from the west — Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake, Aasgard Pass, then across the core Enchantment basin — or from the north and east on the much longer Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail (#1553) into the upper basin.

From the pass the line heads west and up the peak's shoulder. Most of it is walking with occasional use of hands, class 2, along the eastern arm; there is a single steeper step at around 7,900 ft.
hazards: A single steep step on the east arm around 7,900 ft
Snow lingering across the basin approach and the shoulder well into summer
Committing onto the crest toward the southwest summit turns the day into exposed 4th class

name: South Gully
approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (elev. ~3,400 ft) on FS Road 7601 off Icicle Road. Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (Trail #1599) south up the Mountaineer Creek valley through Douglas-fir/subalpine forest, crossing Mountaineer Creek on sturdy footbridges; the grade is moderate for the first 2.5 miles (about 1,500 ft gain) to the signed junction with the Colchuck Lake Trail — go left/uphill. From the junction the trail steepens and grows rockier for another 1.5 miles to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and ~2,280 ft from the TH, lake at 5,570 ft) — the last reliable, easy water source before the high basin. Boulder-hop/skirt the lake's west shore to the boulder field at its south end and the base of Aasgard Pass, a steep, unmaintained talus-and-boulder gully with only faint tread and cairns; it gains roughly 2,000–2,200 ft in under 1.25 miles to the pass (~7,800–7,841 ft) — this is the single biggest approach hazard on the route: loose, shifting rock with real rockfall risk onto parties below, and in early season the gully holds snow/ice that turns it into a steep, exposed snow climb. From the pass, drop gently into the upper Enchantment core basin past Isolation Lake, then traverse cross-country (use-paths and cairns, no maintained trail) through the Tranquil/Perfection/Sigrun/Reginleif lakes tarn cluster toward the Enchantment Peak massif; this route leaves the basin directly between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun and climbs talus to the gully on the peak's south side below the northeast summit, avoiding the longer detour via Prusik Pass. This upper section is class 2–3 talus and slab with sustained exposure in spots; snow lingering into summer can make it markedly harder and is best avoided when icy (some parties instead take the longer, mellower line via Prusik Pass in spring conditions). The route enters fragile alpine terrain in the wilderness's day-use/permit core zone — stay on rock or snow and avoid cutting across meadow or heather. One-way distance to the summit is roughly 7.5–8 miles with about 5,100 ft of net rise from trailhead to summit; counting the drop into the basin and the reclimb to Aasgard Pass on the way out, the round trip comes to roughly 6,650 ft of gain for a car-to-car push (long day; many split it with a camp near Colchuck or in the core zone under permit).
descent: Reverse the ascent line. This route tops out on the northeast summit, which a 2023 survey confirms is the true high point, and its descent is a walk-off: downclimb the short, loose 3rd-class gully off the summit plateau — the same step you came up — then reverse the cross-country traverse back through the Reginleif/Sigrun tarn basin to the top of Aasgard Pass. Downclimbing Aasgard Pass is the descent's main hazard: steep, loose talus that's arguably harder to descend than ascend — plunge-step or downclimb deliberately and stay off snow you can't see the run-out on. Do not glissade the snow-filled sections of Aasgard Pass; several serious and fatal accidents have occurred there from glissaders sliding into hidden moats and sub-snow meltwater channels, especially in early-to-mid season. From the base of the pass, follow the Colchuck Lake shoreline and the Colchuck Lake Trail / Stuart Lake Trail back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route overall — no established rappels on the standard line.
hazards: loose granite blocks and talus
route-finding among the summit's high points
afternoon thunderstorms
lingering snow on shaded benches early season
Aasgard Pass: ~2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/talus in under a mile; a serious fall/SAR hotspot
hidden meltwater channel and collapsing snow bridges on Aasgard Pass in late spring/early summer (at least one fatality reported)

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass and the core basin to the south side
waysIn.season: Late Jun to early Oct snow-free; Apr-Jun normally needs an ice axe for Aasgard Pass and the upper basin
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead on FS Road 7601. Stuart Lake Trail #1599 south up the Mountaineer Creek valley through forest, crossing Mountaineer Creek on footbridges, moderate for the first 2.5 miles to the signed Colchuck Lake junction — go left and uphill. Steeper and rockier for another 1.5 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. That is the last easy water before the high basin.

Skirt the lake's west shore to the boulder field at its south end and the foot of Aasgard Pass and climb the pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under 1.25 miles on faint tread, cairns, loose talus and boulders.

Aasgard has one route-finding rule that matters more than any other and it has killed people. A few hundred feet above the lake the path veers to the climber's left of the creek. Keep left. At the first grove of larches, stay well clear to the left of the rock, whatever the season. At around 6,400 ft stay left of the small cliff band with the waterfall in it, and do not follow any side path toward the waterfall. Drifting right of the trees, toward the waterfall ground, is how parties get cliffed out.

From the pass drop gently into the upper core basin past Isolation Lake and traverse cross-country on use-paths and cairns through the Tranquil / Perfection / Sigrun / Reginleif tarns toward the Enchantment Peak massif. This route leaves the basin directly between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun and climbs talus onto the peak's south side, toward the gully below the northeast summit.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose shifting rock and genuine rockfall risk onto parties below
Getting cliffed out right of the trees / near the waterfall band at ~6,400 ft — fatalities are on record there
Early-season snow and ice turning the pass into a steep exposed snow climb
Sustained exposure on the class 2-3 talus and slab above the basin, worse when snow lingers
Fragile alpine ground in the permit core zone — stay on rock or snow

name: Energizer Bunny
approach: Reached via the standard Core Enchantments approach shared by the other south-face lines: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft), then the south-end boulder field and Aasgard Pass (1.25 mi, ~2,000 ft of steep loose scree — the approach's crux, hazardous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season). From the 7,841-ft pass, travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of Prusik's south face — roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600+ ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country navigation for the final approach.
descent: Same north-side descent as neighboring Solid Gold and Boving-Christensen: find the shared rap anchors on the north side of the ridge and make one full-length rappel (a 60m rope is standard) to easier ground, then scramble/downclimb roughly 30 minutes back around to the base. Anchors are natural (slung blocks/chockstones, webbing/tat), not bolted, and have reportedly been rebuilt/relocated periodically as old tat accumulates in this area — inspect and back up any worn station.
hazards: Dirt/lichen reported on the lower pitches given the route's relative obscurity.

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, to the left side of the south face
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boulder field at the south end, and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft of loose scree in 1.25 miles, hazardous under snow into early July.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way from the trailhead.

Five pitches, about 450 ft: a burly and somewhat dirty roof pitch straight off the deck, an exposed corner to a good ledge, a short aid section through steep ground, a fingery crack between two features, and then the final corner crack shared with the neighbouring line to finish.

Because it joins that neighbour near the top, it shares its descent: a single full-length rappel on the north side and about thirty minutes of scrambling back round to the base.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft of loose scree, with hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
Burly, dirty roof pitch immediately off the ground
Short aid section at mid-height adds rope-management complexity
Dirt and lichen on the lower pitches from little traffic
Shared north-side rappel anchors rebuilt and relocated over the years
Afternoon weather arrives unseen from behind the peak
Long approach

waysIn.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
waysIn.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Prusik Pass and round onto the west face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.
hazards: Long approach, about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain to Lake Vivianne, then past the upper lakes to Prusik Pass
Burly, dirty roof pitch immediately off the ground
Short aid section at mid-height adds rope-management complexity
Dirt and lichen on the lower pitches from little traffic
Shared north-side rappel anchors rebuilt and relocated over the years
Afternoon thunderstorms
waysIn.whyThisWay: Earlier in the season while Aasgard Pass is snowy, or for parties wanting to skip the loose scree grind, at the cost of about two extra miles and a thousand feet of gain.

name: East Gully Route (East Peak)
approach: From the Esmeralda/Ingalls trailhead, cross the North Fork Teanaway River near a jam of small trees, then follow a backcountry route up talus and (early-season) snow slopes to reach the base of the east-facing gully on the East Peak.
descent: From the East Peak summit, down-climb/scramble south down talus and scree for roughly 400-500 ft, then traverse gradually south across slopes to intersect the De Roux Creek Trail and follow it down toward the De Roux trailhead. That trailhead is about a mile down the valley from the road-end Esmeralda/Ingalls trailhead where you started, so finish by walking back up the valley along the North Fork Teanaway road or the unmarked path beside it — effectively a loop rather than a reversal of the ascent gully. In mid-June a trail marked on maps below the East Peak could not be found, so expect to descend off-trail to the De Roux path.
hazards: High rockfall risk in a loose, water-washed gully — helmet essential
Protection is limited to small stoppers/cams on friable rock through the crux
No established rappel line; descent is via down-scrambling talus on the opposite (south) side of the peak

name: Southwest Slope (De Roux Creek)
approach: Start at the De Roux trailhead and campground (~3,800 ft), on the left about 8.5 miles up gravel FR-9737 beyond the end of the paved North Fork Teanaway Road. Take the Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 west, crossing the North Fork Teanaway and then De Roux Creek on bridges. About a mile in, keep right where the De Roux spur branches left, on the trail signed for Gallagher Head Lake. The trail climbs steadily up the valley between Esmeralda Peaks and Koppen Mountain, crosses the creek again on rocks or logs (awkward in snowmelt), passes several waterfalls, and makes its last switchback across a talus ridge at roughly 5,500-5,600 ft, where a house-sized boulder sits beside the tread. Leave the trail there on the boulder's climber's left and head up the hillside on a northeast bearing. Above is about 1,100 ft of sustained Class 2 scree and talus with no marked path; the line beneath the southwest ridge and the talus farther to climber's right both go, and a boulder field farther west is an alternative if the direct slope is too loose. The top 100-150 ft is loose broken rock. The west summit is a walk-up and very slightly higher than the east summit, which is the one the maps mark; most parties tag both. The round trip is about 7 miles with roughly 3,100 ft of gain, and there is no water once you leave the valley trail.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling. Retrace the ascent line down the Class 2 scree and talus slope, aiming back for the trail's last switchback; staying in the trees beside the boulder field on the way down avoids most of the loose talus. Rejoin the Boulder-De Roux Trail at the house-sized boulder and follow it back down the valley to the De Roux trailhead. The east and west summits are close enough to link along the connecting ridge before descending. No fixed anchors or rope work are reported; the hazards are loose rock underfoot, rockfall onto parties below, and finding the right line back to the switchback in low cloud, since the open slopes look alike.
hazards: routefinding among the multiple Esmeralda summits
afternoon thunderstorms
loose talus and scree on the upper ridge
lingering snow on the upper scree slope into early summer
early-season De Roux Creek crossings

waysIn.name: Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 to the last switchback
waysIn.season: July into October. The slope faces south and clears early, though the scree is at its worst fully dry.
waysIn.notes: This is the standard approach. From the De Roux trailhead follow the Boulder-De Roux Trail west up the valley between the peaks and the mountain opposite; at the junction a mile or so in, the left branch is the signed De Roux spur and the way on is the right-hand trail signed for Gallagher Head Lake. That climbs steadily for another mile and a half, topping out at a creek crossing that takes some balance, and passes several waterfalls before making its final switchback across a talus ridge below an open scree field. The Esmeralda Basin trail on the far side of the massif connects to this one only as a long loop by way of the jeep road and the lake, so it is a different way round to the same departure rather than a separate climbing line.
hazards: A sustained scree and talus slope of roughly 1,100 ft with nothing to hold a slip
Navigation through the meadows, tree cover and upper boulder fields is genuinely tricky and many paths lead up with none of them obvious
The upper hundred to hundred and fifty feet is loose broken rock, easy to send down onto a party below
One short section of steeper scrambling has been used to reach the final summit block
Two summits within about ten feet of each other in height, with the maps and the register disagreeing about which is which
No water once you leave the valley trail

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Start at the Entiat River Trailhead (elev. ~3,150 ft) at the end of Entiat River Road (FS Road 51), where a Northwest Forest Pass is required. Follow the Entiat River Trail No. 1400 upstream through mixed forest, gently graded, for about 4 miles. At roughly the 4-mile mark the trail reaches the crossing where a footbridge once stood; the bridge deck burned in the 2015 Wolverine Fire and only the steel I-beams and railing remain, so plan on either crab-walking the exposed beams (some real fall risk, especially with a pack) or fording the Entiat River directly, which can run high and cold with early-season snowmelt — this crossing is the approach's main hazard and should be scouted before committing. Once across, pick up the Cow Creek Meadows Trail No. 1404 and climb steadily northwest through subalpine forest, passing Myrtle Lake (a good water source and camp option) a few tenths of a mile past the river crossing. Continue up-valley into Cow Creek Meadows itself (about 5,000 ft, reached by a steep, sun-exposed climb of roughly 1,300 ft in a mile), an open avalanche-prone basin below the Fifth of July Mountain ridgeline — snow can linger here into July and avalanche debris/downed timber from the slopes above is common, so expect some route-finding through blowdown and brush at the meadow's edges. Above the meadows the trail climbs on to Cow Creek Pass on the mountain's shoulder; leave the trail there and work up open talus and heather slopes on the mountain's south side toward the south ridge, gaining the rest of the height cross-country over scree, boulders and intermittent goat/climber's paths. There is no reliable water above Cow Creek Meadows, so fill up there or at Myrtle Lake. Total one-way distance to the summit is on the order of 8-9 miles with about 4,500 ft of gain, consistent with a long day trip or, more commonly, an overnight basecamp at Myrtle Lake, Cow Creek Meadows, or the Larch Lakes.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: pick your way back down the open south-facing talus, scree and heather slopes off the south ridge to the trail at Cow Creek Pass, watching footing on the loose rock (more hazardous descending than climbing) and staying alert for parties below if scree is being kicked loose. Follow Cow Creek Meadows Trail No. 1404 back down through the meadows, past Myrtle Lake, and rejoin the Entiat River Trail No. 1400 for the roughly 4-mile walk back down-valley to the trailhead. The Entiat River crossing near the old bridge site (burned I-beams or a ford) is again the key obstacle and is often trickier tired and later in the day when snowmelt flows are higher. This is a walk-off/scramble descent with no technical downclimbing and no rappels required under normal summer conditions; a helmet is worth carrying for the loose south-slope terrain, and an ice axe may be prudent for early-season snow patches on the upper mountain or in Cow Creek Meadows.
hazards: remote, multi-mile approach with unreliable-to-nonexistent cell coverage
open-slope, unmarked cross-country routefinding above Cow Creek Meadows
loose talus/scree on the summit slopes
standing burned/downed timber and deadfall on the lower Entiat River and Cow Creek Meadows trails (2015 Wolverine Fire)
sun exposure and limited water on the steep final trail mile into Cow Creek Meadows and on the open summit slopes
lingering snow on north-facing terrain into early July

waysIn.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
waysIn.season: Mid-July through early October, and popular in early autumn for the larch.
waysIn.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.
hazards: No water beyond the stream in the gully below Basalt Pass
Slick pumice where the ridge trail fades out
Scree gully descent off the col and a 500 ft loss into the boulder basin that must be regained
Loose rock and tree debris on the south ridge
Long open ridge fully exposed to afternoon weather
Lingering snow on north-facing terrain into early July
Remote, unreliable cell coverage

waysIn.name: Entiat River and Larch Lakes
waysIn.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the Entiat River road, follow the Entiat River trail up the valley and climb the side trail to the Larch Lakes meadows. From a camp between the lakes the summit is a modest day out along the ridge. Longer than the Basalt Ridge line, but on maintained trail with water, so it suits multi-day trips and loops. The Entiat River side goes by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass; that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe.
hazards: Burned and downed timber on the lower Entiat River and Cow Creek Meadows trails
Footbridge gone at the river crossing near the 4-mile mark
Open unmarked cross-country routefinding above Cow Creek Meadows
Loose talus and scree on the summit slopes
Sun exposure and limited water on the steep final trail mile into the meadows
Lingering snow on north-facing terrain into early July
Remote, unreliable cell coverage
waysIn.whyThisWay: For a multi-day trip or loop, since it keeps to maintained trail with water and lets you camp at the lakes, though it is longer than the ridge line.

name: Fire on the Mountain
approach: From the Mountain Loop Highway, turn onto FR 4096 (Bedal Creek Trailhead spur) and park at the trailhead, 2,790–2,800 ft. Follow the Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old-growth forest along Bedal Creek's steep banks; the maintained tread peters out roughly 1.5–2.5 miles in, at a large brushy washout coming down off the basin below Sloan's West Face. Scramble up the boulder- and blowdown-choked washout — this is the crux of route-finding on the approach — until a cairn marks an exit onto a climber's path (often flagged with pink tape) that switchbacks steeply through forest from about 3,500 ft to 4,900 ft. Above treeline the path crosses talus and a meadow bench (4,900–5,300 ft) with summit views, passes a stagnant tarn near the 5,300 ft saddle between Bedal Peak and Sloan Peak (last reliable water is here or at the cascading streams just below), then continues on rocky, exposed scrambling terrain to about 5,800 ft at the toe of the glacier — crampons/axe may be needed here depending on season. For the Southwest Face (Fire on the Mountain's start), do not follow the standard Corkscrew line onto the glacier; instead cross the low ridge that separates the West Face basin from the Southwest Face basin/meadows to reach the base of the face. Total car-to-base time runs about 3 hours for a fit, familiar party; expect a long day given ~8 pitches of technical climbing still ahead. An alternate approach via the Cougar Creek/North Fork Sauk trailhead (FR 49) converges with the Bedal Creek route around 5,000–5,500 ft but requires fording the North Fork Sauk River, a crossing that is deep, swift, and best avoided solo or in high early-season flow.
descent: From the top of the technical climbing, stash rock gear and follow the upper Corkscrew line roughly 400–500 ft of 3rd/4th class scrambling to the true summit (optional — many parties skip the summit push and head straight for the descent). To descend: return to the gear stash, downclimb a few hundred feet, then drop right down a steep heathered gully to an 'access ramp' — a sound-granite ledge system that is easy 3rd class scrambling over boulders and vegetated steps. Follow the ramp until it necks down to a slabby downclimb. Here parties either continue downclimbing directly to snow (low 5th class, unprotected) or rig one rappel to reach the snowfield below and keep the whole exit at 4th class. Existing rappel tat/anchors have been reported on the ramp system, but they are natural (slung horns/blocks) and of questionable, unverified quality — back them up or build your own rather than trusting them blind. Once on snow, traverse clockwise around the mountain (rope up for any crevassed/glacier travel) back to the Southwest Face basin and reverse the approach. Treat the single rappel as optional/conditions-dependent: in late-season low-snow conditions parties have downclimbed the whole exit with no rope out.
hazards: Low route traffic means lichen, moss, and dirt can be present in cracks.
Descent ledges/glacier remnants can hold snow into midsummer, complicating the scramble finish.

waysIn.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
waysIn.season: Aug-Sep, once the approach snow has cleared
waysIn.notes:
FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead, about 2,790-2,800 ft. Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth along the creek's steep banks; the maintained tread peters out roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in at a large brushy washout below the basin.

Scrambling the washout is the route-finding crux of the approach. Look for a cairn marking the exit onto the climbers' path — it leaves left around 3,500 ft near 48.0560, -121.3631 and is often flagged with pink tape — and follow it in steep forest switchbacks to about 4,900 ft.

Above treeline the path crosses talus and a meadow bench between 4,900 and 5,300 ft, passing a stagnant tarn at the Bedal-Sloan saddle. Last reliable water is there or at the cascading streams just below. The ground beyond turns rocky and exposed toward the glacier toe at about 5,800 ft.

A fit party familiar with the line reaches the base in around three hours. The Cougar Creek / North Fork Sauk trailhead on FR 49 converges with this line between 5,000 and 5,500 ft but adds a ford of the North Fork Sauk.
hazards: Boulder- and blowdown-choked washout at the end of the maintained tread
Steep, exposed scrambling above the meadow bench
Firm snow near the glacier toe early in the season
Ford of the North Fork Sauk if using the FR 49 alternative

name: Fish & Whistle
approach: Same approach as True Grit and Ragged Edge: Sunrise Mine Trail #707 from the Sunrise Mine Trailhead, through Wirtz Basin and Headlee Pass (~4,720 ft, 2.7 mi, loose rock/rockfall in the narrow couloir), down to Vesper Creek and up a short rise to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~4,950 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain — last water), then off-trail up the talus ridge to the Vesper-Wolf col and across the exposed heather ledge system at ~5,800 ft (slick when wet, holds snow into mid-to-late summer — ice axe useful early season). Fish & Whistle's start is not a separate landmark on this traverse — it's a large tree roughly 50 ft left (west) of the True Grit start, on the talus/boulder apron directly below the north face, so simply continue the same ledge traverse slightly past True Grit's start to find it. Plan 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the route.
descent: Fish & Whistle climbs the same upper north-face headwall as True Grit and finishes in the same general area near the top of the face/summit ridge, so the standard exit is almost certainly the same walk-off used for True Grit and Ragged Edge: scramble down the southeast side (a seasonal snow slope early on, open slabs/talus by late summer) back to the Vesper-Wolf saddle, then down to Vesper Lake and out the Sunrise Mine Trail. No rappel anchors or rap-specific beta for this route were found in any published or trip-report account. Given its harder, more sustained bolt-protected pitches, a party unable to finish the walk-off (e.g., benighted or in bad weather) could retreat by rappelling the bolted anchors pitch-by-pitch with a single 60m rope, but this is not the documented standard descent.
hazards: No bridged water crossings on the approach trail; creek crossings can be difficult during high water
Off-trail scrambling sections above Headlee Pass carry real fall exposure
The North Face sees heavy weekend traffic; expect other parties on True Grit and Ragged Edge nearby

waysIn.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep; the ledge traverse holds snow into mid-summer
waysIn.notes:
Identical to True Grit and Ragged Edge. Sunrise Mine Trail #707 from the Sunrise Mine trailhead: log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish, Wirtz Basin, cairned talus, Headlee Pass at about 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles with loose rock and rockfall exposure in the narrow couloir, then down to Vesper Creek and up a short rise to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 4,950 ft and 3.5 miles — last water.

Stay on the summit trail to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, leave it and swing north across the slabs to the saddle with the two large cairns at about 5,700 ft. The heather ledges start about 30 ft above the cairns; traverse west on the goat trail across the north face. Plan three hours or more to the base.
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Slick, exposed heather on the ledge traverse
Snow lingering on the traverse into mid-to-late summer
Runout friction climbing off the deck on pitch 1

name: Southwest Slope (Standard Route)
approach: From Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry (or a floatplane) to Stehekin Landing. Ride the NPS shuttle bus 4.4 miles up Stehekin Valley Road to Harlequin Bridge ($5 fare), cross the bridge, and follow the road past Harlequin Camp and the Stehekin Airport to pick up the Stehekin River Trail. Follow this mostly flat trail southeastward about 3 miles to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction. The Devore Creek Trail then climbs steeply through rock bluffs and open forest for about 1 mile, enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, and traverses brushy, dry hillside for roughly 3 more miles to Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft) — the only designated camp in the area, with room for about three tents. From Bird Creek Camp, most parties do Flora as a long day round trip: bushwhack through open forest (spiderwebs, chest-high brush, and blowdown reported) toward the saddle south of Enigma Peak, then follow the route description above to the summit.
descent: Down-climb the southwest ridge/slope on the same loose talus and scree used for the ascent, back to the saddle south of Enigma Peak, then drop and re-cross upper Castle Creek before regaining the bushwhack corridor down to Bird Creek Camp. The loose, sometimes football-sized talus is reported as noticeably more tedious and unstable on descent than ascent — expect slower travel and watch for rock knocked loose onto climbers below.
hazards: The mountain's rock is a desolate pile of loose gneiss, producing persistently loose footing on the summit talus.
This is a remote, multi-day wilderness approach reachable only via the Stehekin ferry/floatplane and shuttle, with no road access and long potential evacuation times if injured.
One party noted fine volcanic ash accumulation (about 2 inches) at higher elevations, adding to already loose footing.

waysIn.name: Devore Creek Trail from Bird Creek Camp over the Enigma saddle
waysIn.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
waysIn.notes: Come up the lake by passenger ferry or floatplane, ride the shuttle up the valley road to the bridge, cross it and follow the road past the camp and the airstrip to pick up the river trail. Follow that mostly flat trail southeast to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction, then climb steeply through rock bluffs and open forest into the wilderness and traverse brushy, dry hillside to Bird Creek Camp — the only designated camp in that stretch of trail, sitting about fifty yards before the creek crossing, with room for about three tents and a cook area. From camp the peak is a long day of its own; it does not combine with the neighbouring summit above the same camp, and every account allows a full day for each.
hazards: Off-trail navigation with no tread through the woods; two ways to end up in the wrong basin
600 ft descent off the divide into the creek that must be reclimbed on return
Talus degrades from solid boulders to fist-size rock moving underfoot
Loose rubbly gneiss throughout
Access only by Stehekin ferry or floatplane and shuttle; long evacuation
Lingering snow and cornices early season; whiteout navigation
Rockfall from parties above

waysIn.name: Holden Village over Tenmile Pass
waysIn.notes: From Holden, climb to Tenmile Pass, descend the shoulder into upper Riddle Creek, then traverse northeast into the Castle Creek basin to join the standard line around 6,500 ft. Longer and more involved than Devore Creek; mostly used to combine Flora with Riddle Peak, or by parties exiting to Holden after climbing from Stehekin.
hazards: Long, involved route over Tenmile Pass and down into upper Riddle Creek before traversing to Castle Creek basin
Loose rubbly gneiss and shifting talus on the summit slopes
Remote wilderness; long evacuation if injured
Lingering snow and cornices early season; whiteout navigation
Rockfall from parties above
waysIn.whyThisWay: When linking Flora with Riddle Peak, or when finishing out to Holden after climbing from Stehekin; it is much longer than the Devore Creek line.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From Barlow Pass Trailhead (end of pavement on the Mountain Loop Highway, elev. ~2,361 ft, 30.5 mi east of Granite Falls), the approach starts on the gated Monte Cristo Road/Old Monte Cristo Townsite Trail — a flat, easy old railroad grade that parallels the South Fork Sauk River for about 4.1 miles to the Monte Cristo ghost town (elev. ~2,750–2,800 ft). This stretch is closed to public vehicles (maintained by volunteers) and has been damaged by past flood events: the original bridge over the South Fork Sauk near the townsite was destroyed, so expect to either ford a side channel (safe in low water, hazardous during rain/snowmelt) or cross on a fallen log — check current conditions before relying on either. From the townsite, pick up the Glacier Basin Trail, climbing steadily alongside Glacier Creek through forest; roughly the last half-mile below Glacier Basin becomes rough, rocky scrambling near a series of waterfalls (Glacier Falls). Leave the maintained trail around 4,200–4,500 ft, just above the falls, where Glacier Creek is easily and safely accessible — this is the last reliable water before the climb. From there it's cross-country travel: traverse talus and heather benches, then steep, brushy timber, toward Foggy Peak's south face/west ridge. Snowline commonly sits near 5,000 ft into early summer, so an ice axe (and possibly light crampons) is worth carrying for the upper approach in June/early July. The final few hundred feet to the summit is a steep class 3 gully with abundant loose, downsloping rock and some route-finding needed to stay at class 3 rather than straying into class 4 terrain; a helmet is strongly recommended for anyone climbing behind another party member. One-way distance from Barlow Pass to the summit is roughly 8 miles with about 4,000-4,400 ft of cumulative elevation gain, consistent with the ~25.75 km (16 mi) round-trip distance.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — down the same loose class 3 summit gully with care (loose rock and downsloping holds make down-climbing the crux, more than the ascent), then back across the talus/heather benches and through the steep brushy timber to rejoin Glacier Creek and the Glacier Basin Trail around 4,200–4,500 ft, out to Monte Cristo townsite, and back down the old road/railroad grade to Barlow Pass. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required and there are no fixed anchors or rappel stations on this route. In early season, parties often glissade lingering snow patches on the upper mountain where safe to speed the descent, then downclimb the rock below the snowline. The primary descent hazards are rockfall in the loose gully (stay tight as a group and be deliberate about not kicking rock onto anyone below), the slippery/loose scree and downsloping rock on the upper mountain, and the tedious, brush-choked steep forest lower down. Rappels: 0.
hazards: long, multi-stage Monte Cristo approach (gated road, trail, then off-trail scrambling)

routefinding on the off-trail south face/west ridge above Glacier Basin — do not confuse this approach with the Poodle Dog Pass–Silver Lake Trail (#708), a different trail south of Monte Cristo townsite
afternoon thunderstorms build quickly over the Monte Cristo peaks in summer
loose, down-sloping rock and rockfall on the upper south face — helmet required
lingering snow and a steep glissade-able gully on the approach into early summer

waysIn.name: Glacier Basin Trail to the timbered ridge
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the Monte Cristo townsite take the Glacier Basin Trail — not the Poodle Dog Pass trail, which leaves the townsite southward toward Silvertip and Columbia and does not reach Foggy Peak at all. Follow it about a mile and a half, a short distance above the falls, and leave it near 4,200 ft at the point where Glacier Creek is easy and brush-free to reach; that is the last reliable water. There are two traverses on this route with a climb between them, and collapsing them into one is how parties get it wrong. First, cross the creek and traverse nearly level to the base of the timbered ridge. Then climb that ridge — start on its right where there is less brush and shift onto its left side after several hundred feet to avoid small cliff bands, where a game trail helps — carrying on up to anywhere between about 4,800 and 5,300 ft. Lower means more brush, higher means gain you give straight back, and 5,100 ft is the usual compromise. Only then turn left for the second, near-level traverse.
hazards: Brushy sidehill traversing, and small cliff bands on the timbered ridge
Conditions at the gully entrance vary enormously by month — one party met ice-hard snow with deep moats on the right and huge overhangs on the left
The summit gully is steep with abundant loose, downsloping rock — helmets, and do not climb directly beneath one another
Real exposure on the short final scramble off the notch

name: North Ridge
approach: North-northeast via glacier traversals. From Boston Basin parking, hike to Boston Basin high camp (~6400 ft). Traverse moraine and west edge of Quien Sabe Glacier to 7,500 ft. Climb to Sharkfin Col (7,720 ft).
descent: The North Ridge finishes on the summit, and the way off is the West Ridge. Downclimb and rappel the West Ridge to the notch (one rope is enough for the rappels, and several anchors exist, so the mix is a matter of choice), then downclimb or rappel the snow couloir below the notch into Boston Basin; the Cat Scratch Gully to the climber's left is a rappel alternative. Allow more time than expected, because mixed downclimbing and rappelling takes most parties longer than the ascent suggests, and carry an axe for the couloir.
hazards: long exposed ridge
route-finding
glacier approach

Large bergschrund crossed via rappel off Sharkfin Col onto the Boston Glacier; a distinct moat where the glacier meets the North Ridge rock can require careful, sometimes technical negotiation to exit — condition-dependent, harder late season.

Steep snow gully sections on the North Ridge have serious fall consequence -- a slip can result in a long uncontrolled slide/fall onto the Boston Glacier below, so solid snow/ice technique and belays where appropriate matter here

waysIn.name: Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier, then north to the foot of the ridge
waysIn.season: Mid to late summer, for dry rock and a glacier that is still bridged where it matters
waysIn.notes: From the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft on Cascade River Road, the old Diamond Mine roadbed runs about a mile to the mine site, then the climbers' path climbs hard through forest with four stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at about 6,400 ft. From high camp, follow the moraine and the west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier up to about 7,500 ft and climb to Sharkfin Col at 7,720 ft — roughly 10 ft of 5.7 rock and 200 ft of a class 3 gully to gain it, on loose scree underfoot. The col is the commitment. From it you rappel roughly 100-150 ft, in one or two stages depending on snow, down a loose gully onto the Boston Glacier; retreat after that means re-climbing to the col. Traverse north through crevassed ground toward the north end of the glacier, then re-ascend to the ridge. Three Forbidden routes cross Sharkfin Col and use this rappel. Where you leave the Boston Glacier is what separates them.
hazards: A rappel of roughly 100-150 ft (depending on snow) down a loose gully off the col, with rope-snag on loose rock, and no easy retreat once you are down it
A heavily crevassed traverse of the Boston Glacier where a fall would be serious
A distinct moat where the glacier meets the North Ridge rock, sometimes needing technical work to exit, and worse late season
Steep snow gully sections on the ridge itself where a slip runs uncontrolled onto the Boston Glacier
A long, exposed crest with the descent on a completely different side of the mountain

name: Northeast Face
approach: From Boston Basin Trailhead, hike ~3-4 mi via old mine road then a climbers' path (4 stream crossings) to high camp near 6,400 ft (3-4 hrs). Continue along the moraine and west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col (~7,720 ft) via ~10 ft of 5.7 rock and a Class 3 gully. Rappel into the bergschrund on the far side and climb a short ice wall to gain the Boston Glacier, then traverse west across the Boston Glacier to the base of the Northeast Face below a prominent ice patch.
descent: Do not reverse the Northeast Face. Most parties descend by the West Ridge, as below; the East Ledges off the northeast side are the faster but looser, harder-to-follow alternative. From the true summit, downclimb back past the false summit to the crux tower, then work down the West Ridge crest with exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and about 3 rappels off slung horns and blocks, back to the notch between Forbidden and Torment. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to the first station of the Cat Scratch gullies, the parallel rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. About 5 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, off fixed anchors on the rib on the down-climber's left, bring you to the snowfield below the south face. Some stations are deliberately short, so do not skip one, and be ready to build an anchor if you cannot find the next. Early season, while the couloir still holds good snow, some parties descend it instead, rappelling the steepest snow to the moat and downclimbing the rest. From the base, cross back to Boston Basin camp and hike out the climbers' trail. This is a long day; budget extra time given the remote, less-travelled ascent line.
hazards: steep firm ice and mixed terrain
bergschrund at the base
shaded, cold aspect that holds hazard later in the season
remote position with a long, complex retreat
do not confuse this route with the East Ledges (wa_forbidden_peak_east_ledges), the loose ledge-traverse descent on the same aspect that carries a documented 1975 fatality

waysIn.name: Sharkfin Col, the schrund rappel and an ice wall, then west across the Boston Glacier to the ice patch
waysIn.season: Late spring to early summer, when the face still holds the best ice and snow
waysIn.notes:
From the Boston Basin trailhead, three to four miles by the old mine road and the climbers' path with four stream crossings to high camp near 6,400 ft. Continue along the moraine and the west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col at about 7,720 ft, gained by roughly 10 ft of 5.7 rock and a class 3 gully.

The first-ascent party rappelled from the col into the bergschrund and climbed a 15 ft vertical ice wall to get out of it onto the Boston Glacier. Expect the schrund to be the awkward part of the day before the climbing starts.

From the glacier, traverse west — a short traverse, not the long northward one the North Ridge makes — to the base of the face.

This line is climbed rarely enough that no fixed gear should be assumed and modern first-hand descriptions are scarce; treat any description of it, including this one, as an outline.
hazards: A rappel into a bergschrund and a 15 ft vertical ice wall to get out of it onto the glacier
A north-facing ice feature that has thinned over recent decades — verify there is ice deep enough to take a screw rather than assuming it
Everything on the face funnels through the ice patch, so it is the exposed spot for anything released from above
A remote position with a long, complex retreat and a descent by the West Ridge on the far side of the peak
So few ascents that conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic

name: Northwest Face
approach: From Boston Basin Trailhead, hike ~3-4 mi via old mine road then a climbers' path (4 stream crossings) to high camp near 6,400 ft (3-4 hrs), often continuing to a bench at ~7,500 ft beside the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Tower. Ascend the west side of the Quien Sabe Glacier to a notch above Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier below the bergschrund, traverse the heavily crevassed Boston Glacier, then continue around to the north arm of the Forbidden Glacier. Climb ~900 ft of 30-40+ degree snow/ice to reach the base of the technical rock (5.6 knife-edge ridge leading into the 5.8 crux). Most parties treat this as a 3-day trip.
descent: Do not reverse the Northwest Face; descend by the standard West Ridge. From the true summit, downclimb back past the false summit to the crux tower, then work down the West Ridge crest with exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and about 3 rappels off slung horns and blocks, back to the West Ridge notch. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to the first station of the Cat Scratch gullies, the parallel rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. About 5 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, off fixed anchors on the rib on the down-climber's left, bring you to the snowfield below the south face. Some stations are deliberately short, so do not skip one, and be ready to build an anchor if you cannot find the next. Early season, while the couloir still holds good snow, some parties descend it instead, rappelling the steepest snow to the moat and downclimbing the rest. From the base, cross back to Boston Basin camp and hike out the climbers' trail. This means NW Face parties do not re-cross the Boston or Forbidden Glaciers or re-climb Sharkfin Col on the way down.
hazards: mixed snow/ice/rock
route-finding on a big face
shaded, cold aspect

Two crevassed glaciers before the climbing starts: up the west edge of the Quien Sabe to about 7,500 ft, then a 150 ft rappel down a loose gully off Sharkfin Col onto the Boston Glacier and an ascending traverse across it. A large crevasse opens around 7,600 ft in many seasons and can cost real time. The rappel is the commitment — retreat means re-climbing to the col — and the face tops out at a cornice near 8,375 ft.

waysIn.name: All the way round to the Forbidden Glacier's north arm
waysIn.season: Mid summer, for the best balance of firm ice and dry rock
waysIn.notes: This is the hardest-to-reach established line on the peak and most parties treat it as three days. The recorded approach goes the long way round: from the Boston Basin trailhead, three to four miles by the old mine road and the climbers' path with four stream crossings to high camp near 6,400 ft, often pushing on to a bench near 7,500 ft beside the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Tower. Ascend the west side of the Quien Sabe to the notch above Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier below the bergschrund, traverse that heavily crevassed glacier, and continue around to the north arm of the Forbidden Glacier on the mountain's other side. Other parties reach the same basin without the Boston Glacier at all — by dropping west off the North Ridge line, by rappelling from the West Ridge notch over crevasses and moats, or over Torment Col. All of them end in the same place. From the north arm, about 900 ft of 30 to 40-plus degree snow and ice leads to the base of the rock.
hazards: Two crevassed glaciers before any climbing, with a large crevasse that opens around 7,600 ft in many seasons and can cost real time
A committing rappel off Sharkfin Col — retreat means re-climbing to the col
A moat or bergschrund where the snow pulls back from the foot of the rib
A shaded, cold aspect that holds hard ice late, and a face that tops out at a cornice near 8,375 ft
A descent on a completely different side of the mountain, by the West Ridge couloir

name: West Ridge
approach: From the Boston Basin trailhead off Cascade River Road, follow the unsigned but well-beaten Boston Basin climbers' path. It starts by following the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about 1 mile, then splits off the roadbed to climb steeply and directly through forest. The trail crosses four seasonal creeks/streams (reliable water) as it switchbacks up through increasingly open timber, breaking out above treeline around 5,300 ft. Above treeline it continues into the broad boulder-and-heather Boston Basin cirque, past the usual high-camp sites around 6,300–6,600 ft (roughly 4–5 miles and 3–4 hours from the car, ringed by Sahale, Sharkfin Tower, and Mt. Torment). From camp, make an ascending traverse across talus and the Quien Sabe Glacier remnant toward Forbidden's south face; when the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is often a faster, drier alternative to crossing snow/ice. Rope up if the glacier is crevassed or snow-covered. Aim for the obvious ~500-ft snow-and-ice couloir splitting the left edge of the south face — the standard gully leading to the West Ridge notch. This couloir steepens to 40–50°+ near its top, typically wants crampons/axe (and sometimes a picket) into mid-summer, and is guarded by a moat near its top, against the rock walls approaching the notch, that can require a short steep step or a band of loose rock to surmount. Exiting the couloir at the ridge-crest notch is roughly 4–5 hours and about 4,500 ft above the trailhead.
descent: There is no walk-off. Descend the way you came up as far as the notch, then take the rock gullies beside the couloir. From the true summit, downclimb back past the false summit to the crux tower, then work down the ridge crest with exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and about 3 rappels off slung horns and blocks, back to the West Ridge notch. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to the first station of the Cat Scratch gullies, the parallel rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. About 5 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, off fixed anchors on the rib on the down-climber's left, bring you to the snowfield below the south face. Some stations are deliberately short, so do not skip one, and be ready to build an anchor if you cannot find the next. Early season, while the couloir still holds good snow, some parties descend it instead, rappelling the steepest snow to the moat and downclimbing the rest. Watch for the moat again at the bottom. From the base, reverse the glacier-remnant and talus traverse back to Boston Basin camp and out the climbers' trail to the trailhead. The descent is usually slower than the climb: parties report about 1.5 hours back down the ridge to the notch against about 1 hour up it.
hazards: serious exposure on the knife-edge crest
rockfall in the access couloir, worse late season
afternoon thunderstorms
icy or hard snow in the couloir early season

Glacier crossing from Boston Basin to reach the couloir, then a lower and an upper bergschrund at its base — the lower is usually stepped across and the upper turned on the left. Late season the snow pulls away from the rock into a deep moat, and what is left of the glacier opens into moat-like slots straight down to rock.

This is the most heavily travelled route on the peak, and it has had fatal accidents: an unroped fall of about 90 ft on wet slabs above the upper bivy by a climber who had taken off their helmet (August 2018), a fall while rappelling the descent gully after rockfall (2013), and a fall into a crevasse off the end of a rappel rope with no backup (July 2017). Stay roped on wet or loose rock, back up every rappel with an autoblock and knots in the rope ends, and keep your helmet on until you are off the descent.

waysIn.name: South face couloir to the West Ridge notch
waysIn.season: Jun–early Aug, while it still holds snow
waysIn.notes: From the Boston Basin high camp, traverse up and east across talus and the remains of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Forbidden's south face. Where the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is usually faster and drier than staying on snow; where it is snow-covered or crevassed, rope up. The couloir itself runs about 500 ft and steepens to 40–50° near the top, which is where crampons and an axe stop being optional. Reaching the notch is roughly 2,000 ft above camp.
hazards: A moat where the snow pulls back from the rock guards the top of the couloir. Expect a short steep step or a band of loose rock to get over it, and expect it to be worse the later in the season you go.
Rockfall once the sun reaches the couloir — parties above are the usual source, so it pays to be off it early.
40–50° snow near the top, on ground where a slip does not stop on its own.

waysIn.name: Cat Scratch gullies (late season, once the couloir has melted out)
waysIn.season: Late Aug–Sep, dry conditions
waysIn.notes: When the couloir has gone to loose talus and scree, the usual line moves off the snow onto the rock gully system immediately west — climber's left — of it. Roughly the first 200 ft is class 4, easing to grassy class 3 for the last 200 ft to the notch. It is loose the whole way, and it is slower than it looks on the approach.
hazards: Loose rock from bottom to top. Keep the party out of one another's fall line rather than spread across the gully.
The parallel gullies are easy to confuse, and committing to the wrong one puts you on the ridge away from the notch with loose ground to traverse back.
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late summer, once the couloir has gone icy, rocky and prone to rockfall, and the rock gullies to its west offer a surer way to the notch without a snow-to-rock transition.

name: Southwest Face
approach: From Trinity Trailhead (2,800 ft) at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR 6200, follow the Buck Creek Trail (#1513) roughly 9-9.5 miles, climbing through forest, an old avalanche debris field (~4,500 ft), and past an unmarked junction with the Pass No Pass way-trail (bears right, ~5,800 ft). Continue up the way-trail to Pass No Pass (~6,400 ft) and the alpine camping benches beyond, from which Fortress's southwest face and south ridge come into view. Note: storm damage has closed FR 6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground (about mile 16), adding roughly 7 miles of road-walking each way before even reaching the trailhead; check its status with the Wenatchee River Ranger District.
descent: From the summit, retrace the ascent line down the south ridge / upper southwest face. The direct gully is the loosest ground on the mountain; a 2015 party found and cairned an alternate class 3 line over more solid, blocky terrain to skier's right of the gully that later parties have followed. Continue down through scree and talus to the grassy benches above Pass No Pass, back over the pass, and down the Buck Creek Trail to Trinity Trailhead. Descending the southwest face to Pass No Pass is easy until the burned forest on Buck Creek, where blowdowns and a high-log river crossing near 3,300 ft slow the walk out.
hazards: Rockfall from loose talus and scree on the southwest face gully, especially with other climbers above.
Steep snow slopes on the approach into early summer requiring ice axe self-arrest skills.
River/creek crossings and brushy, sometimes-indistinct trail sections lower on the approach.

waysIn.name: Buck Creek Trail #1513 and the Pass No Pass way-trail
waysIn.season: Jun-Oct, best Jul-Sep once the south-west face has melted out; an axe and sometimes crampons for early-season snow on the approach slopes below the pass
waysIn.notes:
From Trinity Trailhead at 2,800 ft, follow Buck Creek Trail #1513 roughly nine to nine and a half miles, climbing through forest and an old avalanche debris field near 4,500 ft.

The turn is the thing to watch for and it is not marked: an unmarked junction with the Pass No Pass way-trail bears right at about 5,800 ft. Follow the way-trail to Pass No Pass near 6,400 ft and the alpine camping benches beyond it, from which the face and the south ridge come into view.

Storm damage has closed FR-6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground around mile 16 (check its status before you go), adding roughly seven miles of road-walking each way before you even reach the trailhead.

From a high camp in the Pass No Pass basin, parties report about three and a half to four hours up and two and a half to three back.
hazards: The direct south-west gully is the loosest ground on the mountain and is directly above anyone below
Steep snow on the approach slopes below Pass No Pass into early summer, needing self-arrest skills
An unmarked way-trail junction at about 5,800 ft that is easy to walk past on a nine-mile approach
Creek crossings and brushy, indistinct trail lower down
Roughly seven extra miles of road-walking each way while FR-6200 is closed beyond Atkinson Flat

name: East Slope Route (Headlight Basin)
approach: From the Esmeralda Trailhead, hike the Esmeralda Basin Trail and Ingalls Way Trail up to Ingalls Pass (~6,500 ft), then traverse into Headlight Basin below the Ingalls/Fortune ridge.
descent: Parties climbing while snow still covers the slope (typically into late June) often descend by glissade — roughly 1,000 ft of glissading has been reported back toward camp. Once the slope has melted out later in summer it becomes loose talus/scree requiring careful downclimbing. From the base of the slope, reverse through Headlight Basin, over Ingalls Pass, and back down the Esmeralda Basin Trail.
hazards: Steep snow slopes below the summit ridge through June
Loose talus/scree hazard once snow melts out
Wind exposure on the open summit ridge

name: Standard Route (Esmeralda Basin – Lake Ann Pass)
approach: From the Esmeralda Trailhead (#1394, 4,269 ft), hike the Esmeralda Basin Trail (shared with the Lake Ingalls/Ingalls Way trail for the first 0.4 mi), then stay on the Esmeralda Basin Trail past the Ingalls Way junction to the trail toward Lake Ann. At the trail junction below the pass, head up toward Lake Ann and the saddle above it, then leave maintained trail and follow the ridge boot path to the summit.
descent: The drop from the summit ridge back down to the pass above Lake Ann is steep and, especially early in the season, can remain snow-covered well into summer — downclimb carefully or glissade only after checking the runout. Below the pass, rejoin the maintained Lake Ann trail and Esmeralda Basin Trail for the hike back to the Esmeralda Trailhead.
hazards: Loose, rocky scrambling terrain along the summit ridge
Afternoon thunderstorms and strong wind exposure on the open ridge
Lingering steep snow near the Lake Ann pass in early season increases fall risk without an axe

name: Southwest Route
approach: Four Brothers sits on Chikamin Ridge in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and the standard approach starts at the Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331, ~2,375 ft), reached via SR 903 north from Cle Elum ~17 mi, then Cooper Lake Rd/FR-46 roughly 9-10 mi to the signed trailhead. From the trailhead the trail drops briefly to a crossing of the Kachess River, then climbs to a junction with the Little Kachess Trail (#1312) at about 0.25 mi. Around 1.3 mi it passes an old mine site and shortly after crosses Mineral Creek itself, entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary. The next stretch runs high above the creek through old-growth forest and several brushy former avalanche paths - expect deadfall and slow going here, especially early season. Near the 4-mile mark the trail crosses a side creek (the last dependable water before the basin) and then climbs steeply, gaining roughly 1,500 ft in the final mile-plus to Upper Park Lake (~4,900 ft, about 5.4 mi from the trailhead). From the Park Lakes basin, leave the trail and go cross-country up mixed heather benches and slabby rock toward the saddle on Chikamin Ridge - the four cliffy summit points of the Four Brothers are unmistakable and form steep, technical terrain that should be flanked rather than climbed directly from below. Once on the ridge crest, traverse back to the base of the southwest-facing gully/slope system that gives this route its name, roughly 6.5-7 mi and about 4,000 ft of gain from the car. Expect lingering snow in the gully well into July, loose stacked talus higher up, and real routefinding complexity picking a line through the pinnacle/cliff-band maze - this is the part of the outing that most often proves the crux, more so than any single move. From the high saddle on the Glacier Lake trail, follow the ridge and bear right after about 300 ft of climbing onto class 2 ledges that lead to the crest.
descent: Most parties reverse the ascent line: down the southwest gully/heather slopes back to the Chikamin Ridge saddle, then back around the Four Brothers' cliff bands into the Park Lakes basin and out the Mineral Creek Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - no fixed rappel stations are documented on the Southwest Route itself, and parties who stay on the described line generally do not need to rope up for the descent. Treat any exposed Class 3 downclimbing sections with care, particularly on wet or lichen-covered rock, and a short handline (30-60 ft) is a reasonable option for a party uncomfortable downclimbing the crux step. Note that the adjacent, better-documented Chikamin Peak has a known single-rope bail rappel off its summit horn used by parties who prefer not to downclimb its Class 3 chimney; that anchor is on Chikamin's line, not this route, but if you drift onto that terrain by mistake it's a known escape option. Because Four Brothers' summit block is a genuine cluster of cliffy pinnacles, poor visibility or late-day descent meaningfully raises the chance of wandering onto steeper terrain than intended - budget enough daylight to descend the correct gully rather than improvising a line off the pinnacles. Dropping directly toward Glacier Lake works at class 2, but heather and boulders slow the bottom; it saves little over reversing to the saddle.
hazards: loose rock, especially on ledges and the summit block(s)
route-finding among the multiple summits
unmaintained boot path off the PCT with several cliff bands to thread around
steep dirt/heather ('veggie belay') downclimbing near the ridge crest
lingering snow/ice in NE-facing gullies and bowls (e.g., near Glacier/Iceberg Lakes) into July

waysIn.name: Park Lakes basin to the Chikamin Ridge crest
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Mineral Creek Trail from the signed trailhead: the Kachess River on logs or a wade, past the old mill site, across Mineral Creek at the wilderness boundary, then a long traverse high above the creek through old-growth and a string of grown-in avalanche paths where brush and deadfall make for slow going. Ford the tributary creek near four miles — the last dependable water before the basin — and grind the steep pitch above it into the Park Lakes benches. Stay on the trail to the pack camp where it meets the Pacific Crest Trail, then leave it and climb heather benches and rock slabs cross-country.
hazards: Loosely stacked talus high on the route
Snow lingering in the gully well into July
Route-finding among four separate rock points that all look like summits from below
Steep heather and dirt near the ridge crest
Cliff bands and pinnacles that have to be threaded rather than climbed

name: South Route
approach: Start at the Goodell Creek trailhead (~600 ft, off Hwy 20 near Newhalem, North Cascades NP/Ross Lake NRA). Follow the old roadbed/climbers' path paralleling Goodell Creek for about 4 miles, gaining only ~1,000 ft, to a junction around 1,700 ft marked by a stone/rock arrow, post, and large cairn — this is the standard jump-off for every Southern Pickets objective and the last easy, reliable water before the climb steepens. Here the unmaintained Terror Creek climbers' trail cuts uphill to the right and turns relentlessly steep: a boot-beaten but often faint path gains roughly 4,000-4,700 ft in well under 3 horizontal miles through old-growth forest and brush (expect head-high slide alder/devil's club depending on season and snow year) before breaking out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft onto heather benches, slabs, and snowfields. From treeline, rather than stopping at Terror Basin (the camp used for McMillan/Inspiration/Terror objectives), continue a rising traverse west/northwest staying near the 5,800-6,400 ft band into Crescent Creek Basin — the standard high camp for Frenzel Spitz, Himmelhorn, Ottohorn, and the Chopping Block, reached via a steep initial drop into the basin on mixed snow/talus followed by a roughly one-hour traverse. From camp, climb east/northeast onto the ridge to gain the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col; the south (Crescent Creek) side of this col is the comparatively friendlier side — loose but moderate 3rd/4th class scrambling — in contrast to the sustained loose 5th-class terrain that guards it from the north. From the col, downclimb/scramble roughly 500 ft down broken, frequently snow- or ice-covered terrain on the north (Frenzel Spitz) side to reach the base of the South Route proper. There is no dependable water above the Terror Creek junction until snowmelt or tarns near camp, so carry enough for the ~4,500+ ft, multi-hour climb in between; the ~18-mile round-trip distance reflects that this is realistically a long day-and-a-half approach with a basin camp, not a single push.
descent: Reverse the approach line: from the Frenzel Spitz summit, downclimb/scramble back down to the base of the connecting gully and climb back up the ~500 ft of broken, loose terrain to regain the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col. On the way in, the descent from the col onto its north side drops into a broken couloir and glacier/moat terrain — anchors reported here are natural (a pin, sling, and/or nut equalized in a crack or around a block), not bolted or chained, so be ready to build or back up your own and treat any fixed tat as suspect. Parties commonly need one rappel to get down the steepest ice/rock step directly below the col; a single 60m rope has been reported as sufficient, though in icy or early-season conditions some parties have needed a second, shorter rappel or have downclimbed a lower-angle step instead of rappelling it. Below the rappel, expect further downclimbing across broken glacier and moat terrain — this is a real late-season hazard: test snow edges carefully before committing weight, and be ready to use an ice axe to climb out of moat pits, since the glacier edges near the col have been described as unable to hold body weight. Once back on the col, descend its friendlier south side into Crescent Creek Basin, then retrace the approach traverse and descend the steep climbers' path back down to the Goodell Creek roadbed and trailhead.
hazards: chronically loose, rotten Pickets rock — significant rockfall danger to the party and anyone below
moats and steep snow at the Ottohorn–Himmelhorn col, especially early season
extreme remoteness — multi-day approach with no quick bailout and no cell coverage
sustained Class 3 exposure on 'The Barrier' during the approach
brushy, faint approach trail and a Terror Creek crossing that can be hazardous at high water

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Creek path, past Terror Basin to a Crescent Creek Basin camp, then over the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Goodell Creek trailhead at about 600 ft off Hwy 20 near Newhalem. Follow the old roadbed and climbers' path along Goodell Creek for about 4 miles, gaining only about 1,000 ft, to a junction around 1,700 ft marked by a stone arrow, a post and a large cairn. That junction is the standard jump-off for every Southern Pickets objective and the last easy, reliable water before the climb steepens.

The unmaintained Terror Creek climbers' trail cuts uphill to the right and turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 4,000-4,700 ft in well under 3 horizontal miles through old-growth forest and brush, with head-high slide alder and devil's club depending on the season, before breaking out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft onto heather benches, slabs and snowfields.

From treeline, rather than stopping at Terror Basin, continue a rising traverse west-northwest staying near the 5,800-6,400 ft band into Crescent Creek Basin, reached via a steep initial drop into the basin on mixed snow and talus followed by roughly an hour of traversing.
hazards: Head-high slide alder and devil's club on a relentlessly steep unmaintained path
No dependable water for roughly 4,500 ft of climbing
Broken, frequently snow- or ice-covered ground on the 500 ft descent to the route's base
The north side of the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col is a rappel proposition with glacier and moat terrain below it
Glacier edges near the col have been described as unable to hold body weight late season

name: Full Tilt (Tempest Wall Free Version)
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), take the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) to Colchuck Lake — 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek at 1.5 miles, turning left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet (2.5-3 hours, last water). Continue around the lake's west shore to the boulder field at its south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min, holds wet snow into July), then cut climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Full Tilt — the free version of the Tempest Wall's aid line(s) — starts a few hundred feet down the gully to the right of the West Face's start, on Grade III terrain. Expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final scramble to the wall.
descent: Full Tilt climbs the Tempest Wall and finishes over the top. Continue to the summit ridge and use Colchuck Balanced Rock’s standard walk-off: class 3-4 scrambling around the summit block to a sandy scree gully, with one optional rappel of about 30 m off a slung horn on the east side, then clockwise around the peak to the base, about 50 minutes. The Tipping Point, on the same wall, has a bolted two-rappel bail line from its Sky Lounge belay into the approach gully; plan on the walk-off rather than rappelling Full Tilt itself.
hazards: Loose rock typical of the formation

name: South Slopes
approach: From the Wolf Creek Trailhead (large parking area at the end of FS Road 5505 above Winthrop; Northwest Forest Pass required) follow Wolf Creek Trail #527 up-valley into the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. The trail drops roughly 250 ft in the first stretch, then settles into a long, gently-graded valley-bottom walk. About 90% of this corridor burned in the 2021 Cedar Creek Fire, so expect standing dead snags and blackened deadfall the entire way in — a real overhead-hazard concern in wind, and the cause of at least one reported tree-fall near camp. At roughly 2.6 miles the trail fords the North Fork of Wolf Creek (can run high in early season) — treat this as your last easy, reliable water source if you're moving fast. The Abernathy Lake trail splits off around 7.6 miles; continue straight up the Wolf Creek valley. The trail opens into Gardner Meadows around 9.5–10.3 miles (roughly 2,400–2,800 ft of cumulative gain from the trailhead), a broad, wildflower-and-lupine-filled basin at about 5,700 ft that serves as the standard base camp, with running water and (in season) avalanche lilies. From the meadows, leave the maintained trail and climb cross-country up the west side of the small stream draining south off Gardner Mountain, staying on its west bank; terrain shifts from broad grassy benches to scree and talus. Around 6,200 ft you reach a small meadow basin below the peak — from there work up toward the summit ridge, threading a few short cliff bands and gullies. This stretch is the route-finding crux of the approach: loose rock underfoot, and into early summer, lingering snow patches that can warrant an ice axe. The final approach to Gardner's 8,902 ft summit is class 2–3 scrambling on broken rock and scree.
descent: This is a non-technical alpine scramble — the standard West Ridge / Saddle Traverse descent involves no rappelling (0 rappels). From Gardner's summit the route continues west along the summit ridge over a false summit, then descends steeply through loose scree and (early-season) snow to a saddle below Point 8487. From that saddle, the crest up to Point 8487 has gendarmes and cliff bands that go at class 3-4 if taken direct, while the ridge from Point 8487 on to North Gardner Mountain is generally class 2; if conditions look sketchy (wet rock, verglas, or lingering snow), the safer line is to drop off the ridge to about 7,400–7,500 ft and side-traverse around the cliff bands before regaining the ridge near Point 8487. Most parties climb Gardner first and North Gardner second, then reverse the route: descend North Gardner's scree back toward the saddle and drop Gardner's south-facing scree/talus slopes back to the small stream basin and Gardner Meadows — trip reports specifically recommend this order, since Gardner's scree descends quickly and pleasantly (good scree-skiing when dry, glissade potential when snow-covered), whereas doing it in reverse is reportedly 'miserable.' From Gardner Meadows, retrace Wolf Creek Trail #527 roughly 10.3 miles back to the trailhead, including a final, easy-to-underestimate ~200 ft climb right near the trailhead. Carry an ice axe into early July for the one or two snow patches typically encountered high on the traverse, and watch for burned/standing dead timber the entire way, especially in wind.
hazards: routefinding on the connecting ridge
afternoon thunderstorms
loose, exposed Class 2-3 rock and lingering steep snow on the crest between Point 8,487 and North Gardner
2021 Cedar Creek Fire burn scar along ~8 miles of approach: standing dead hazard trees, especially in wind, and almost no shade
difficult early-season ford of the North Fork Wolf Creek at ~2.3 miles
lightning risk on the exposed summit (a summit register was reportedly destroyed by lightning)

waysIn.name: Gardner Meadows: west bank of the stream to the scree
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From Gardner Meadows around 5,700 ft leave the maintained trail and get onto the west side — climber's left — of the small stream draining south off Gardner Mountain toward Wolf Creek, then climb the steep meadows paralleling it, staying west of the streambed the whole way. A small meadow basin arrives at about 6,200 ft. Keep working toward the ridgeline; at roughly 7,100 ft the meadows give out and the ground turns to loose, marble-sized scree over sand, which is the slog that defines this route — about 1,400 ft of gain in half a mile. A faint bootpath exists in places and is easy to lose. Reckon on four to five hours from the meadows.
hazards: Standing dead snags and blackened deadfall the length of the burnt Wolf Creek corridor
1,400 ft of loose scree over sand — poor footing in both directions
Lingering snow patches in the cliff bands and gullies into early summer
Loose, exposed scrambling with gendarmes on the connecting ridge if you carry on to North Gardner

name: Gato Negro
approach: From the pullout, find a faint boot path descending loose talus/scree to the east into the trees, passing a trail register, then crossing Early Winters Creek on a log (~4,080 ft). The trail climbs the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, steeply gaining elevation to a basin/camp bench around 6,500 ft (roughly 2 hours from the car), where the trail continues on up to Burgundy Col (~7,720 ft). Whine Spire, just south of the Wine Spires, is reached from the bench rather than the col: branch right toward Silver Star and climb to the toe of the middle of the three rock masses to the right of the col. Good camping and a late-season spring are near 6,400-6,500 ft.
descent: The descent does not reverse the route. Make a few rappels over the top of the spire into the steep gully between Whine Spire and the west summit of Silver Star, then work down the gully with long sections of loose 4th-class downclimbing and a few more rappels. The gully is extremely loose, with rock coming down through it constantly, so keep the party out of one another's fall line and clear of the ropes. Do not attempt it in rock shoes. Plan on 2.5 to 3 hours in good conditions; parties benighted here describe about three hours of complex route-finding in the dark, and advise against starting it after dark.
hazards: Loose rock throughout, especially on descent
Fragile granite features requiring careful body placement
Runout sections on poor rock quality
Route-finding challenges despite relatively straightforward path

waysIn.name: Burgundy Creek bench to the base of Whine Spire
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: Whine Spire is a sub-peak on Silver Star Mountain's north ridge, south of the line of Wine Spires and below Silver Star's west summit, and its face is reached from the upper Burgundy Creek basin below Burgundy Col. From the pullout on SR-20 a few miles east of Washington Pass, take the boot path down to Early Winters Creek, cross on the log near 4,080 ft, and climb the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek to the bench camp near 6,500 ft. From the bench, branch right off the col trail toward Silver Star and climb to the toe of the middle of the three rock masses to the right of the col; the route starts right of a big yellow scar. Expect a short patch of firm snow at the base and, later in the season, awkward scree-filled moats where the snow has pulled back from the rock.
hazards: Steep snow patch and scree-filled moats at the base
Runout 5.8 sections on loose granite
A 5.9+ offwidth chimney section high on the route
Twelve long pitches, most 180 ft or more — a full day for most parties

name: South Route
approach: Ghost Peak sits deep in the Northern Pickets, just south of Crooked Thumb Peak and about 0.3 mi NNE of Phantom Peak, so this is a multi-day wilderness approach, not a day hike to a base. Standard access is from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FR 32, ~3,100 ft); the alternative from Ross Lake, up Big Beaver Creek and Wiley Ridge, also reaches the Challenger end of the Northern Pickets. From the Hannegan Trailhead, follow the Ruth Creek Trail over Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft, ~4 mi in) and drop into the Chilliwack River valley to a forest camp near Copper Creek/Graybeal Camp (~8 mi in). Day two crosses the Chilliwack River on the cable car and climbs the steep, brushy Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass (~5,210 ft, ~16 mi in) - the last maintained trailbed before the range proper. From Whatcom Pass the route leaves the trail: rope up for glacier travel across the Whatcom Glacier (or go up and over Whatcom Peak's north ridge) to Perfect Pass (6,300 ft), then continue over the Challenger Glacier and Solar Pass to a moraine high camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier, directly below Ghost Peak's south face - roughly 23-24 mi and three days in.
