From that camp, a roped glacier crossing reaches the base of the peak, where the original 1970 line climbs low-5th/Class 4 rock up the south face and south arete before finishing on the west face; route-finding here is the crux in poor visibility, since Ghost Peak, Crooked Thumb, and Phantom Peak all crowd the same skyline. Overall hazards: early-season fords on the Chilliwack River, real crevasse risk on the Whatcom and Challenger Glaciers, and loose, exposed ground near the high camp that's easy to lose in cloud.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the south face/south arete/west-face traverse used on the first-ascent route back to the notch below the summit horn, then continue down snow and talus to the high camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Ghost is a small, generally solid rock horn; expect to downclimb the way you came, with no fixed or bolted anchors anywhere in this remote sub-range. Carry a rope and a small rack of slings/nuts in case the exposure or wet/icy rock make a short rappel preferable off a natural anchor (slung horn or chockstone) near the top of the arete; a single 30m rappel would be more than enough to protect the steepest section if needed. Treat this as a walk-off/downclimb route with a possible single natural-anchor rappel in reserve, not a route with a defined multi-rappel descent. Once back at camp, reverse the full approach: back over Solar Pass and the Challenger Glacier, over Perfect Pass/Whatcom Glacier or Whatcom Peak's north ridge to Whatcom Pass, then down the Brush Creek Trail, back across the Chilliwack River and over Hannegan Pass to the Hannegan trailhead.
hazards: snow/glacier on approach
loose rock
remoteness

waysIn.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier camp to the notch south of the peak
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: Ghost is climbed from the high camp shared with Crooked Thumb and Phantom, all three being within a few tenths of a mile of each other. From that camp a roped glacier crossing reaches the foot of the peak. The original line gained the notch south of the peak, and gained it from the west rather than by attacking the notch directly from the glacier below, then stayed on the south and west sides of the mountain following obvious weaknesses at easy-to-moderate fourth and low fifth class. Access from camp is described as obvious once you are established there; the difficulty is knowing which of the three summits you are under.
hazards: Crevasse risk on the Whatcom and Challenger Glaciers on the way in, and on the crossing from camp
Loose, exposed ground near the high camp that is easy to lose in cloud
Three summits crowding one skyline — route-finding is the crux in poor visibility
Early-season fords on the Chilliwack River on the approach

name: Meade Glacier
approach: Drive to the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead (Trail #1120, elev. ~4,044 ft): from Naches, WA take US-12 W about 22 miles, turn onto Forest Road 1200 (Tieton Reservoir Road) for 4.5 miles, then onto Forest Road 1000 (South Fork Tieton Road) for 12.6 miles to the trailhead at road's end (last ~7 miles gravel, generally in good condition). Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows (crossing Conrad Creek) into the Goat Rocks Wilderness, continuing to the Surprise Lake loop. Take the loop's right fork to the trail's high point, then leave the trail and climb west into a basin; pass between a pair of big mounds and descend briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the short, loose scramble to the small saddle and follow the goat and boot path on the southwest side back to the ridge. Descend the Meade Glacier snowfields past the rock band that splits the upper and lower glacier; glissading is common in early and mid season when the snow is consolidated (self-arrest gear required). Recross the basin to the trail's high point, then follow the Surprise Lake loop and Trail #1120 back through Conrad Meadows to the trailhead.
hazards: Steep snowfield below the summit requires solid self-arrest skills.
Loose rock on the summit scramble creates rockfall risk for parties climbing close together.
The Meade Glacier is receding but can still harbor hidden crevasses/moats in early season.
Long, remote approach (~20 miles round trip) with limited water in late-season dry years.

waysIn.name: Conrad Meadows and the Surprise Lake loop to the Meade Glacier
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Drive to the Conrad Meadows and South Fork Tieton trailhead at road's end, about 4,044 ft, reached by the Tieton Reservoir road and then the South Fork Tieton road off the highway west of Naches. The last several miles are gravel.

Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows, crossing Conrad Creek, into the Goat Rocks Wilderness and on to the Surprise Lake loop. Take the loop's right fork to the trail's high point, then leave the trail and climb west into a basin. Pass between a pair of big mounds and descend briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.

This is a long day: roughly 20 miles round trip with real gain, and limited water late in a dry season.
hazards: A steep snowfield below the summit requiring solid self-arrest
Loose rock on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk between parties climbing close together
A receding glacier that can still hide crevasses and moats
A long, remote round trip of roughly 20 miles with limited water in a dry year
Basin navigation that depends on visibility once off the trail

name: West Route
approach: Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (Chambers Lake area) off Forest Road 21/2150 on the west side of the Goat Rocks: turn east onto FR 21, continue about 13 miles, turn at the Snowgrass Trail/Chambers Lake sign onto FR 2150, then follow signs to the Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (elev. ~4,650 ft). Hike Trail #96 (Snowgrass) roughly 4 miles and ~2,000 ft of gain along Goat Creek toward Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow that is closed to camping (use the established sites below it); from there reach the PCT (via Trail #96 or the cutoff Trail #97) and follow it southbound about 2 miles to Cispus Basin, which has an established camp in the trees just above the PCT's Cispus River crossing. Climb to the saddle at the basin's northeast end, then scramble east across the Goat Ledges/Goat Ribs traverse toward Gilbert Peak (often combined with Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak in one traverse day).
descent: Downclimb the Class 2-3 summit section back through the notch behind the black prow, then carefully retrace the white aggregate band across the Goat Ribs/Goat Ledges at the same ~7,500 ft traverse elevation used on ascent to minimize rockfall exposure to teammates below. From the saddle, descend into Cispus Basin, follow the PCT back to Trail #96 (or the cutoff Trail #97), and descend Trail #96 to the trailhead.
hazards: Significant rockfall potential on the Goat Ribs/Goat Ledges traverse, especially with parties stacked at different elevations.
Loose andesite/pyroclastic breccia and tuff throughout the upper mountain.
Steep, sketchy sections on the approach to the summit block reported even in late-season dry conditions.
Route-finding error risk — the correct line depends on identifying the white aggregate band correctly.

waysIn.name: Snowgrass Flats and the Goat Ledges traverse to the black prow
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the ledges are dry
waysIn.notes:
Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat trailhead in the Chambers Lake area on the west side of the Goat Rocks, at about 4,650 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Hike Snowgrass Trail #96 roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft along Goat Creek to Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow; the flat itself is closed to camping, so camp at the established sites below it.

From camp, head cross-country and scramble east across the Goat Ledges and Goat Ribs — a series of rock ribs and shallow gullies — at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft toward Gilbert Peak. This is often combined with Old Snowy and Ives in a single traverse day.

A lower variation holds a consistent traverse elevation of about 7,500 ft, which reduces exposure to rockfall knocked down by other parties.

The route is regarded by some as loose and dangerous. Careful route-finding along the correct band and on goat paths is what makes it a reasonable class 4 passage rather than a bad one.
hazards: Significant rockfall on the Goat Ribs and Goat Ledges traverse, worst with parties stacked at different elevations
Loose andesite, pyroclastic breccia and tuff throughout the upper mountain
Steep, insecure sections approaching the summit block even in dry late-season conditions
Route-finding failure — the whole route depends on correctly identifying the white aggregate band
A class 4 downclimb through the notch on the way back, on the same loose ground

name: Frostbite Ridge
approach: Two approaches are used, both longer and more involved than the standard Sitkum route. (1) Via the White Chuck River, no longer usable since a 2003 flood destroyed the trail and road: the old line followed the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about 6 miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail 1.7 miles up to the PCT. Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing (water) to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT on Glacier Ridge about 0.7 miles beyond the creek, which climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder. (2) Via North Fork Sauk Trailhead: North Fork Sauk Trail to White Pass (~9 miles, ~5,900 ft), then a long traverse north on/near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area — a 20-mile-plus approach day used by some parties. From high camp, the route proper begins by traversing the upper southwest slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to an 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers. Ascend the Kennedy Glacier — a 'crumbling mess' of loose moraine and boulders low down — to an 8,800 ft saddle where Frostbite Ridge proper begins. The ridge itself mixes loose pumice/dust scrambling on narrow, exposed steps with sections of steep snow (45–50°) protected with pickets or ice screws, passing directly beneath/through the Rabbit Ears — twin eroded lava pinnacles — where loose rock is a real hazard, especially in warm, dry conditions (cold, snowy conditions lock the rock in place and make the scramble more manageable). Above the Rabbit Ears the route steepens further into a section of alpine ice, anywhere from a single ~40-foot ice step to roughly 200 feet of AI2, typically simul-climbed with ice screw protection, before crossing the crater rim and descending briefly into the crater to reach the 10,550 ft summit.
descent: Frostbite Ridge is essentially a one-way, committing line — once on the ridge there is no turning back — and virtually all parties descend a different, easier route rather than reversing the ridge. The standard descent is down the Sitkum Glacier: from the summit, descend the gully east of the summit into the upper Sitkum Glacier, traverse and descend to a saddle at roughly 8,000 ft, then continue down the lower Sitkum Glacier to Boulder Basin, picking up the climbers' path back to the PCT, then south on the PCT to White Pass and down the North Fork Sauk Trail to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead (some parties instead reverse to the Cool Glacier/Gerdine Ridge side if that's where their car is staged). The single rappel belongs to the ridge itself rather than to this walk-off descent: there is a natural belay-horn anchor (a rock horn, typically backed by old slings — inspect before trusting) just above the steep ice north of the Rabbit Ears, used to lower one pitch of steep ice into a notch referred to as the 'doorway gap' in the summit rib. This is a single-pitch rappel — a 30m single-strand rope is sufficient for the drop described — encountered while working through the crux ice/rock step near the Rabbit Ears (i.e., on the way up for most parties, since the standard descent avoids the ridge entirely); some parties simul-climb this step with screw/picket protection instead of rappelling, depending on ice conditions. Carry 3–4 ice screws and/or pickets for this section and for the steep snow/ice above the Rabbit Ears regardless of whether you end up rappelling it.
hazards: Long, committing ridge in a very remote setting

The 'Rabbit Ears' — twin rock gendarmes gained by two steep ~40m snow pitches; parties typically cross in front of the West Ear, traverse below it on the south side (2nd-3rd class), and descend to a saddle behind the East Ear
Steep snow/ice to ~50° and a short ice/mixed crux
Cornices on the ridge and crevasses on the Kennedy/Scimitar glaciers

waysIn.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the 7,200 ft camp
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The White Chuck River Trail was destroyed by a 2003 flood and has no road or trail access, so this approach is no longer usable; reach Kennedy Ridge from White Pass on the PCT instead. The old line ran from the White Chuck River trailhead at about 2,300 ft. Follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about six miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail about a mile and three quarters to the PCT.

Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing, which is your water, to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the trail on Glacier Ridge about two thirds of a mile beyond the creek. That path climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder.
hazards: Road access on the White Chuck side has long-running problems and the river trail is gone, so this way in is likely unusable
Unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT
Loose moraine and boulders low on the Kennedy Glacier
Crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
Very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
Steep snow/ice to ~50 degrees, cornices on the ridge
Committing ridge with no easy retreat; remote
waysIn.whyThisWay: Only if the White Chuck road and trail are ever rebuilt; since the 2003 flood it has been closed, so it is not a realistic choice and most parties take the Sauk route.

waysIn.name: Suiattle River Road and the PCT via Milk Creek
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Drive the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from Darrington to the vehicle closure at milepost 12, then walk or bike the last 11 miles to its end at Sulphur Creek Campground. Follow the Suiattle River trail about seven miles to the bridge over the river, then the PCT southbound about nine miles to a camp in the East Fork Milk Creek basin at about 5,600 ft. From there continue up the ridge on snow and pumice to the same standard high camp near 7,200 ft.

The Suiattle River Road has a long history of flood damage and multi-year closures, so its status is worth confirming rather than assuming.
hazards: Repeated flood damage and long closures on the Suiattle River Road
Very long PCT approach day
Crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
Very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
Steep snow/ice to ~50 degrees, cornices on the ridge
Committing ridge with no easy retreat; remote
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the Suiattle River road is open and a party prefers the north side, though its trails are poorly maintained and the road has repeatedly flooded out.

waysIn.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then north
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes: Some parties use the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass — about nine miles and 5,900 ft — and then make a long traverse north on or near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area. It is a twenty-mile-plus approach day and is chosen when the other two roads are out.
hazards: Twenty-mile-plus approach day
Crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
Very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
Steep snow/ice to ~50 degrees, cornices on the ridge
Possibly unstable old rappel slings at the Rabbit Ears
Committing ridge with no easy retreat; remote

name: Kennedy Glacier
approach: Standard historical approach: from the White Chuck River Trailhead (FS-23, closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 after flood damage; check status), follow trail #643 about 4 miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the PCT; turn left (north) and follow the PCT about 2 miles to the Glacier Creek crossing and campsites (pack-in time 4-5 hours). An alternate approach via the North Fork Sauk Trail and PCT over Red Pass to Glacier Creek is also used and is the open option while FS-23 stays closed.
descent: Besides reversing the ascent line, the standard alternate descent goes via Frostbite Ridge: traverse past the distinctive 'Rabbit Ears' rock formation, then descend the (separate) Vista Glacier back down to the lower Kennedy Glacier and Kennedy Ridge camp, watching for opened crevasses and softening snow bridges throughout.
hazards: Upper Kennedy Glacier is heavily crevassed — described in trip reports as a 'mazed mess' of 5-15 ft crevasses requiring careful, deliberate routefinding
Seracs on climber's left near the Kennedy Peak wall, where some parties set belay anchors on exposed glacial ice
Staying left to simplify crevasse navigation trades off increased rockfall exposure from Kennedy Peak above

Long, remote wilderness approach; the old White Chuck trailhead has been cut off since March 19, 2025, when FR 23 was closed from milepost 3.7 (no end date given on the Forest Service alert updated June 30, 2026), so parties start at the North Fork Sauk trailhead

waysIn.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
waysIn.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.
hazards: Walk in may be far longer than the mileage because the road is closed at milepost 3.7
8,200 ft of gain from the trailhead
Upper glacier is a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses needing slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left under the Kennedy Peak wall
Hugging the left wall trades crevasses for rockfall from Kennedy Peak
Bergschrund at the glacier head, possibly only one bridge
Remote; long, difficult evacuation
waysIn.whyThisWay: Only when the White Chuck road is repaired and open; it is the short historic way to the Glacier Creek camps but has been closed since the 2003 flood.

waysIn.name: North Fork Sauk and the crest trail north
waysIn.notes: Walk the North Fork Sauk trail up the valley and climb to the crest trail near White Pass, then follow it north past Red Pass, across the White Chuck basin and on toward Kennedy Creek, descending to the bench below the glacier. Long, with real elevation loss on the way, but this is how most parties now reach the Kennedy side.
hazards: Long approach with real elevation loss on the way to the bench below the glacier
Upper glacier is a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses needing slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left under the Kennedy Peak wall
Hugging the left wall trades crevasses for rockfall from Kennedy Peak
Bergschrund at the glacier head, possibly only one bridge
Remote; long, difficult evacuation

name: Sitkum Glacier
approach: From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (off Sloan Creek Road, FR 49), follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 up the valley through old-growth forest, past the Red Creek bridge to Mackinaw Shelter, then up a long series of switchbacks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly 8-9 miles from the car. White Pass and its camp are a short way south along the PCT; this route does not go there. Turn north on the PCT and cross Red Pass (about 6,500 ft) a mile or two on, then descend into the upper White Chuck valley and follow the PCT down it for roughly 7-9 miles, past the old White Chuck River Trail junction (~3,850 ft), to a forested campsite near 4,100 ft beside Sitkum Creek. There, leave the maintained trail on the unsigned, unmaintained climbers' path (closer to a rough angler's path than a real trail), which goes straight up the forested ridge south of Sitkum Creek to Boulder Basin (5,500-6,000 ft), where the trees break and the standard high camp sits on heather and rock benches with running water nearby. From camp, ascend snowfields southeast onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. The old approach up the White Chuck River Trail past Kennedy Hot Springs to the same PCT junction is no longer usable: the White Chuck Road (FR 23) is closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7, and the trail has been listed as inaccessible since the October 2003 flood. Going out, the PCT climbs back up the valley and over Red Pass before the long descent to the car.
descent: This is a walk-off/glacier descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the pumice Sitkum ridge back to the ~9,500 ft saddle east of Sitkum Spire, then descend the Sitkum Glacier's upper section, staying in the corridor left of the icefall/rock rib that splits the glacier's lower half, back down to Boulder Basin. Crevasses exist on the Sitkum but are sparse and generally avoidable with standard route-finding; a rope, harness, and a few pickets are still standard kit. From Boulder Basin, follow the steep climbers' path back down to the PCT at Sitkum Creek, then walk the PCT back up the White Chuck valley and over Red Pass to the North Fork Sauk Trail and the trailhead.
hazards: Very long, remote approach — multi-day commitment far from any road
Crevasse navigation on the Sitkum Glacier
Steepening snow to ~40° below the summit pinnacles
Loose pumice and rock high on the route once melted out

waysIn.name: North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass
waysIn.season: Jun-Aug
waysIn.notes: The way in since the White Chuck side closed. North Fork Sauk Trail #649 runs up the valley through old growth to Mackinaw Shelter and then switchbacks steeply to the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly eight to nine miles from the trailhead. Turn north on the PCT, cross Red Pass a mile or two on, and descend into the upper White Chuck valley, following the PCT down it for roughly seven to nine miles past the old White Chuck River Trail junction to Sitkum Creek. It is much longer than the old approach, and the climb back over Red Pass comes on the way out.
hazards: very long approach on the PCT with substantial gain and loss
no signed junction for the climbers' path

waysIn.name: White Chuck River Trail #643 (closed since the 2003 flood)
waysIn.season: Jun-Aug
waysIn.notes:
This was the standard way up Glacier Peak until the October 2003 flood. The White Chuck Road (FR 23) is now closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 and the trail has been listed as inaccessible since the flood, so this is kept as a record of the old line rather than as a way in.

From the trailhead at about 2,350 ft the trail runs upstream through old growth, crossing Pumice, Glacier and Kennedy Creeks — reliable water, but high with snowmelt in early summer. At about five and a half miles is the old Kennedy Hot Springs area at around 3,300 ft, still a popular campsite; the pool, lodge and guard station were destroyed by the 2003 flood and never rebuilt, so there is no usable hot pool there.

Another mile and a half brings you to Sitkum Creek and the PCT junction at about 3,850 ft. Turn north on the PCT for about half a mile to a forested camp near 4,100 ft.
hazards: road closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 and trail listed as inaccessible
creek fords running high with early-summer snowmelt
steep unmaintained climbers' path with no signage leaving the PCT
crevasses on the Sitkum
waysIn.whyThisWay: Only if the road and trail are restored; it is the old, much shorter standard approach, but flood damage has closed it, so parties now walk in from the North Fork Sauk.

name: South Ridge / Standard Scramble
approach: From the Goat Mountain Trailhead (day-use parking just off FS-32/Hannegan Pass Rd, ~2.1-2.3 mi up from the Glacier Public Service Center), follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It's a well-built but relentlessly steep trail that gains the ridge via dozens of switchbacks, crossing a small cascading creek/waterfall repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock (look for ~100-year-old fire-scarred cedar snags). Around 1 mi (~3,200 ft) the grade eases and the trail traverses onto a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly 2 mi the trail crosses into Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur ('Old Goat Trail') splits east toward an old lookout site - stay on the main tread. Big views of Baker, Shuksan, and Sefrit open through meadows by 2.7 mi, and the maintained trail tops out on the ridge crest at a 5,200-ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft (~4.1 mi, ~3,100 ft gain). Beyond this point the route leaves maintained tread and becomes an open ridge boot path: continue about 0.8 mi and 1,000 ft more to the ~6,600-ft West Peak false summit. Snow lingers here well into summer (reports note solid snow from ~4,300-4,500 ft), so carry an ice axe from around that elevation upward, and expect crampons or snowshoes to be useful in early/late season. Do not push straight over the false summit's top - it corniced and exposed; bypass it on the south or west slope. Past the false summit the ridge drops roughly 300 ft into a notch/col, then climbs the final stretch of mixed snow, rock, and short exposed steps to the true (East) summit at 6,892 ft. A narrow, moderately exposed knife-edge-ish section near the top is the crux of the scramble - keep the axe in hand and self-arrest-ready on the steep snow. There is no reliable water source beyond the creek crossings in the forest (roughly the first 2.5 miles of trail); carry what you need for the ridge and summit push.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route - reverse the ascent line exactly. Downclimb the mixed snow/rock crux back to the col, climb back over (or bypass around, staying off the cornices) the West Peak false summit, and regain the boot path down to the official trail terminus near 5,600 ft. From there, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673's switchbacks back down through the meadows, past the wilderness-boundary/Old Goat Trail junction, and through the old-growth section to the trailhead. Carry an ice axe and know self-arrest for both directions of travel on the snow sections: afternoon sun can soften the snowfields significantly (increasing slip and post-holing risk on the way down), while morning refreeze can leave the same slopes firm enough to want careful cramponing. Give cornices along the ridge crest a wide margin on the way down as well - they are easy to underestimate from above and have caused parties to detour off-route.
hazards: loose rock on the final ridge, especially near the true (east) summit
lingering snowfields on the ridge crest into early-mid summer — small patches noted by hikers even into early July
steep, sidehill unmaintained boot path beyond the trail's end, with real fall exposure
black bears frequent the area — proper food storage is required in Mount Baker Wilderness
open ridge crest offers no bail options if thunderstorms build

waysIn.name: Goat Mountain Trail #673 to the end of maintained tread, then over the West Peak false summit
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow lingers on this ridge and reports have found solid snow from 4,300-4,500 ft well into summer
waysIn.notes:
From the Goat Mountain Trailhead, day-use parking just off FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Road) about 2.1-2.5 miles up from the Glacier Public Service Center, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It is well built and relentlessly steep, gaining the ridge by dozens of switchbacks and crossing a small cascading creek repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock.

Around a mile in, near 3,200 ft, the grade eases and the trail traverses a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly two miles it crosses into the Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur — the Old Goat Trail — splits east toward an old lookout site. Stay on the main tread.

Meadows and big views open by 2.7 miles; the maintained trail tops out on the crest at a 5,200 ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft.

Beyond that it is an open ridge boot path, about 0.8 mile and 1,000 ft more to the West Peak false summit near 6,600 ft, and then on to the true East summit.

There is no reliable water beyond the creek crossings in the forest, roughly the first 2.5 miles of trail.
hazards: Cornices on the West Peak false summit, invisible from above
Solid lingering snow from 4,300-4,500 ft upward well into summer
A knife-edge-ish exposed section near the true summit
No reliable water beyond the forest creek crossings (about the first 2.5 miles)
An unsigned spur trail near the wilderness boundary that leads to an old lookout site instead

name: Southwest Route
approach: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Rainy Pass (4,880 ft) near milepost 158, about 35 miles west of Winthrop or 51 miles east of Marblemount. Park at the Rainy Pass North (PCT) trailhead. Hike north on the Pacific Crest Trail through forest and switchbacks to Cutthroat Pass (~6,800 ft), continue past Granite Pass (~6.25 miles in, where snowfields can linger into August) and along a cliff-cut trail toward Methow Pass. About a mile before Methow Pass, a small, unsigned spur trail switchbacks up to Lower and then Upper Snowy Lake (~6,700–7,000 ft) — roughly 10–11 miles and 2,700 ft of gain one-way from the trailhead. Good campsites sit in the meadow near the lakes.
descent: From the summit, most parties make a single short rappel (roughly 40 ft; a 30m rope is plenty) off the summit block to regain the ridge, then downclimb/scramble class 2–3 scree and talus back toward Snowy Lakes — plunge-stepping the loose scree speeds this considerably. From camp, retrace the PCT approach back over Granite and Cutthroat Passes to Rainy Pass.
hazards: Loose rock and scree are the primary objective hazard on the approach gully and summit block.
The exposed traverse/mantle onto the true summit carries real consequences despite its short length.
Afternoon thunderstorms are common on the exposed upper ridge in summer.

waysIn.name: Rainy Pass PCT over Cutthroat and Granite Passes to the Snowy Lakes spur
waysIn.season: Jul-Oct, with late September and early October favoured for larch colour and stable weather
waysIn.notes:
Drive SR-20 to Rainy Pass at 4,880 ft near milepost 158, about 35 miles west of Winthrop or 51 miles east of Marblemount, and park at the Rainy Pass North PCT trailhead.

Hike north on the Pacific Crest Trail through forest and switchbacks to Cutthroat Pass at about 6,800 ft, continue past Granite Pass at roughly 6.25 miles, where snowfields can linger into August, and along a cliff-cut trail toward Methow Pass. About a mile before Methow Pass, a small, unsigned spur trail switchbacks up to lower and then upper Snowy Lake at about 6,700-7,000 ft. Roughly 10-11 miles and 2,700 ft of gain one-way. Good campsites sit in the meadow near the lakes.

Two pitches. This is also the peak's overall first ascent line, made in September 1946.
hazards: Snowfields lingering at Granite Pass into August
A cliff-cut section of trail beyond Granite Pass
Loose class 2-3 scree and talus on the upper mountain
A 10-11 mile approach before any climbing
Little reliable water between Cutthroat Pass and Snowy Lakes

name: Megalodon Ridge
approach: Start at the Bridge Creek Trailhead on Highway 20 near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass (paved lot on the north side of the highway at about 4,400 ft), where a short connector trail crosses the highway to the Pacific Crest Trail, and head south on the PCT. Follow the PCT roughly 9-10 miles, descending along Bridge Creek, to the junction with the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail near North Fork Camp. Continue about 2 miles up this increasingly brushy trail along the North Fork of Bridge Creek and leave it at an obvious clearing before Grizzly Creek. From there it's off-trail travel: a steep, sustained bushwhack through slide-alder and timber to gain the toe of the long East Ridge ("Megalodon Ridge"), which sits close beneath Goode Glacier's lower icefall. Total approach is on the order of 12+ miles with several thousand feet of gain before any roped climbing begins, so most parties treat this as a multi-day trip and bivy low on the ridge (water is reliable along Bridge Creek and its tributaries but scarce once you're up on the rock, so tank up before leaving the creek). Watch for hidden cliff bands in the brush and general route-finding difficulty in the alder - a faint boot-path or 'tunnel' through the brush, when found, saves considerable effort over thrashing blindly uphill.
descent: Descend the standard Mount Goode line: from the true summit, downclimb and traverse the connecting ridge/notch system toward Black Tooth Notch, the deep gap short of the summit block. This section is done in three single-rope rappels - the first drops fairly directly down the ridge crest, but the second and third are traversing rappels that trend skier's-right/rappeller's-left, so keep the rope's uphill end free and watch for pendulum swing. A 60m rope doing 30m rappels is standard; anchors along this stretch are mixed - some fixed tat/slings on horns and blocks, some natural gear anchors - so inspect any in-place webbing before trusting it. From Black Tooth Notch, three additional rappels (also ~30m on a 60m rope) drop more or less straight down the fall line of the Southwest Couloir; watch for tat marking the stations. That's six rappels total to get off the technical terrain. Once the couloir eases to class 3, if it cliffs out, move climber's left onto easier ground and then traverse back right into the basin beneath the gully; cairns and a climber's path lead down and out (looker's right) to the Park Creek Trail. Because the standard descent drops into the Park Creek/Stehekin drainage - the opposite side of the mountain from the Bridge Creek approach used to reach Megalodon Ridge - getting back to a car at the Bridge Creek Trailhead is a long second act: parties hike down the Park Creek Trail to the Stehekin valley road and back up Bridge Creek on the PCT to the highway, about 20 miles of trail beyond the descent proper. Loose rock in the couloir, rockfall risk from parties above, and aging/sun-bleached fixed webbing at some stations are the main descent-specific hazards.
hazards: very long sustained ridge
remote deep-NCNP position
route-finding over many towers
benightment risk
mostly simul-climbed with sparse belayed pitches — limited protection over long sections
very few documented repeats, so beta and bail options are thin

waysIn.name: Off the Bridge Creek trail to the toe of the arete descending northeast off the main ridge
waysIn.season: Late summer, August into September, once the approach bushwhack and the glacier are most passable; a long committing route that wants a stable weather window
waysIn.notes:
From the Bridge Creek Trailhead on Highway 20 near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass at about 4,400 ft, head south on the Pacific Crest Trail roughly nine to ten miles down Bridge Creek to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp, then up the increasingly brushy North Fork trail.

About two miles up it, leave the trail at an obvious clearing before Grizzly Creek and bushwhack steeply through slide alder and timber to the toe of the arete. Carrying on past Grizzly Creek to the ford and the slabs beside the waterfall leads to the Goode Glacier and the Northeast Buttress, not to this ridge.

The total approach is on the order of twelve or more miles with several thousand feet of gain before any roped climbing. Most parties bivy low on the ridge; water is reliable along Bridge Creek and scarce once you are on the rock, so tank up before you leave the creek.

The first ascent climbed its first fifth-class pitch at dusk and bivied on a bench, with the real difficulty starting the next morning.
hazards: Hidden cliff bands inside the brush
A very long sustained ridge — 2,800 to 3,000 ft of climbing with about 5,000 ft of exposure on one side and 4,000 on the other
Mostly simul-climbed with sparse belayed pitches, so long sections carry limited protection
Very few documented repeats, so beta and bail options are both thin
Benightment on the ridge is a real risk, and the standard descent drops into the Park Creek drainage on the far side of the mountain

name: Northeast Face
approach: South on Pacific Crest Trail along Bridge Creek for 9.6 miles to North Fork Bridge Creek Trail junction; then north with final bushwhacking to glacier base camp
descent: The shared standard descent off Goode (used for this route as for the Northeast Buttress) is down the Southwest Couloir. From the summit ridge, downclimb/rappel a short sequence of stations to Black Tooth Notch — these first rappels trend more sideways/traversing than straight down, so expect some rope-snag risk and use care feeding rope; a single 60m rope is sufficient at every station. From the notch, continue with additional single-rope rappels down into the SW couloir proper (parties commonly report 5-6 total rappels between the summit and the base of the couloir), after which class 3 downclimbing takes over. Anchors throughout are natural — slings and cord around horns, blocks, and chockstones rather than bolts — so carry a few extra feet of 7mm cord/webbing and rap rings to back up or replace weathered tat. Where the couloir narrows and ends in cliffs lower down, exit left onto easier terrain and traverse back into the basin below the gully rather than rappelling the waterfall band beneath. From the base of the couloir, descend scree/talus back into the Goode Glacier basin and reverse the approach (re-cross the glacier, descend the watercourse/slabs, then the North Fork Bridge Creek drainage) to the PCT and trailhead. Given the sustained steep snow/ice character of the upper face on this route and the overall remoteness, treat icefall/rockfall in the couloir and crevasse hazard on the glacier as the primary descent-day objective hazards.
hazards: mixed snow/ice/rock
remote position deep in NCNP
very long approach
route-finding
moat crossing and a steep (50°+) ice step guarding the Goode Glacier approach/exit onto the face, worse late season
sluff-scoured ice after freeze-thaw cycles
cornices near the summit ridge in spring/early summer

name: Southwest Couloir
approach: From the Bridge Creek/PCT trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159 (just over a mile east of Rainy Pass, ~4,400 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound along Bridge Creek. This stretch loses elevation steadily — roughly 1,600 ft over about 9.5-9.6 miles — down through forest to the North Fork Camp junction, where the PCT crosses Bridge Creek (a footbridge here has been washed out in past years; check current NPS conditions before counting on it). At the junction, turn onto the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail and head upstream (north); this climber's/stock trail is roughly 7 miles long and regains about 1,700 ft, but grows progressively brushier and less maintained the farther up-valley you go, with alder and overgrowth becoming a real time sink in late summer. The trail eventually peters out in the big cirque below Goode, Storm King, and Mount Logan — most parties leave the maintained tread around mile 13-14 of the approach to ford the North Fork (a cold, sometimes knee-deep crossing; easier a short way upstream near a cairn) and pick up an intermittent boot path/cairns through talus and alder ('tunnel' sections of brush) toward the toe of the Goode Glacier. From there it's off-trail travel over moraine and glacier remnants (light crampons/axe useful if there's residual snow or open crevasses) to a rotten, blocky ridge that accesses the base of the couloir proper — expect loose, moving rock underfoot on this last stretch. Reasonable bivy options exist near the glacier toe (~6,400-6,800 ft, limited flat tent sites) or higher on ledges closer to the couloir base. Total approach is commonly done as a long day-plus-camp, on the order of 15-16 miles and 4,000-4,800 ft of gain to high camp; water is generally available at regular intervals along Bridge Creek and its tributaries but can be scarce higher up near camp, so fill up at the last reliable stream.
descent: Descend the same Southwest Couloir used on ascent, after rappelling into it from the summit. From the summit area, downclimb broad class 3-4 terrain in the couloir, staying alert for a band of more solid darker rock on the left side (locally called the 'black stairs') which offers cleaner downclimbing than the surrounding rotten rock; the couloir is otherwise loose and rockfall-prone, so groups should descend close together or one at a time through narrows. Lower down, if snow still fills the gully (common into mid-summer), this is a fast plunge-step or glissade; late-season parties will instead pick through talus and scree for several hundred feet. The couloir's mouth opens onto cliffy ground above a waterfall, so exit left (climber's left) onto easier heather benches rather than continuing straight down into the cliffs — this is the one real route-finding crux of the descent. Below that, drop into heather meadows around 7,700 ft where running water is usually found, then retrace the approach line back down through the brush and along the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail and PCT to the Bridge Creek trailhead. The top of the descent is a rappel line, not a downclimb: from the summit, three single-rope rappels reach Black Tooth Notch, and three more drop straight down the fall line into the couloir; a 60 m rope is enough. Below those, the couloir is the scramble and downclimb described above.
hazards: loose rock and scree in the couloir
very long approach
route-finding to the summit
rockfall funnel in the couloir, worse with multiple parties on route
route-finding through the Black Tooth Notch and across the upper Northeast Face traverse

waysIn.name: The cairned ledge into the gully, and the black stairs inside it
waysIn.season: Late June through September depending on snow and ice in the couloir; an axe and crampons are often wanted for the gully approach even in summer
waysIn.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159 (about 4,400 ft), just over a mile east of Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound along Bridge Creek — losing roughly 1,600 ft over about 9.5 miles through forest — to the North Fork Camp junction, where the PCT crosses Bridge Creek. A footbridge there has been washed out in past years, so check NPS conditions rather than counting on it.

Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail, roughly seven miles regaining about 1,700 ft, growing brushier as you go until it peters out in the big cirque below Goode, Storm King and Mount Logan. Around mile 13-14 ford the North Fork — easier a short way upstream near a cairn — and pick up an intermittent boot path and cairns through talus and alder, including tunnel sections through the brush, toward the toe of the Goode Glacier.

Some parties deliberately stay on moraine and talus rather than the glacier basin, because of icefall and audible rumbling from the seracs. Bivy near the glacier toe around 6,400-6,800 ft, or higher on ledges closer to the couloir. The whole approach is commonly 15-16 miles and 4,000-4,800 ft to high camp.

This is the peak's original route, first climbed in 1936, and it is also the descent for the Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge — so expect to meet parties coming down it.
hazards: A rockfall funnel: the couloir is loose and gets worse with multiple parties on it
Receding hidden-glacier snowbridges below 8,000 ft on the way to the gully
A demanding headwall of largely terrible rock near the top
Active rockfall and icefall noise from the Goode Glacier seracs beside the approach
A mouth that opens onto cliffy ground above a waterfall — the one real route-finding trap of the descent
